approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
approach_variants.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs nearly level for the first mile and then climbs at a steady grade to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. Drop off the east side and continue down into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail proper. The tread loses height past a backcountry camp to the Chilliwack River crossing - historically a hand-pulled cable car, and a serious ford if it is not running, so check its status before you plan around it - then runs down-valley past further camps to the Bear Creek confluence. The camp at that confluence has been closed since fire came through the drainage, so confirm it is open rather than assuming a bed there.

At Bear Creek the maintained trail ends. Ford the creek, which can be a genuinely committing crossing in snowmelt, and climb steep brushy timber eastward; higher the brush turns to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows above Ruta Lake. Traverse the divide from there, skirting the loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points and crossing a rock rib, to a broad saddle at about 6,480 ft with running water and heather tent sites. Most parties split this over two days.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the Chilliwack crossing has dropped and the buttress is dry
hazards: a river crossing that depends on a cable car being in service
the Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
steep brushy timber and slide alder with no tread
loose south-facing traverse slopes below the divide points
rockfall and icefall out of the shrinking glacier in the couloir
a moat between neve and slab that worsens through the season
a position days from any road, on either side of the border
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route begins by losing height, and that is the single most important thing to know at camp. From the 6,480 ft saddle you drop down steep scree, trending climber's right, and cross several minor gullies to reach the toe of the small glacier remnant spilling out of the couloir below the buttress. Any line that climbs upward from the saddle toward rock is the wrong one.

Identify the saddle first: it is broad, it has running water on it and flat heather sites, and it sits on the north-west ridge with the wall around the corner rather than above you. A saddle with no water and no camping is not it.

At the ice, the positive test is which side of the buttress you go up. This route climbs the glacier or neve on the climber's-left side of the buttress and then works into slabs that lead to a corner system - the corner is where the technical climbing starts. The toe of the buttress itself, where the rock meets the ice on the right-hand side, is the start of the direct and not of this route. If you are roping up at the very bottom of the rock rather than walking past it on snow, you are on the harder line.

Watch the join between snow and rock. A moat opens where the neve pulls away from the slabs and it deepens through the season; getting out of it onto the slabs is often the awkward move of the approach and it is worth an axe and crampons even in high summer.

A cross-check once committed: the climbing above the corner runs up to about 5.10 with the hardest move an offwidth part-way up, and it finishes on the buttress top, from where a scramble gains the true summit. If your first pitch off the ice is already at your limit, you have started too low and too far right.

approach_variants.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
approach_variants.notes: There is a far shorter line to the same camp from the road on the Canadian side of the border - a fraction of the distance the Hannegan approach covers. It crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, and this page cannot say that crossing is lawful, so confirm it with the border authorities before planning on it; and the tread turns unmaintained and badly overgrown after the first mile or two, so the miles it saves are not all easy ones. Most parties starting in the United States take the long way rather than deal with it; parties already north of the border have the opposite calculation.
approach_variants.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
hazards: an international border crossing on foot, with the documents and permissions that implies
unmaintained and heavily overgrown tread for most of the distance
the same loose divide traverse and the same glacier remnant beneath the buttress
a rescue that may involve two countries
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The approach variant changes only how you arrive at the 6,480 ft saddle. Once there, everything is as for the long approach: the camp is the broad saddle with running water and heather sites on the north-west ridge, and the route starts by dropping off it on steep scree, trending climber's right, across several minor gullies to the toe of the glacier remnant beneath the couloir.

The same two tests apply at the ice. Go up the snow on the climber's-left side of the buttress into the slabs and the corner system. If you are tying in at the very toe of the rock where it meets the ice on the right, you are under the Direct.

And the same negative marker: gaining height straight from the saddle toward rock means you have not gone far enough down. The wall is below and around the corner from camp, not above it.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
approach_variants.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 climbs to Hannegan Pass near 5,100 ft, then drops off the east side into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail. Past a backcountry camp the trail reaches the Chilliwack River crossing, historically a hand-pulled cable car and a serious ford without it, then continues down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence, where the maintained trail ends. The camp there has been closed since fire came through, so confirm rather than assume.

Ford Bear Creek, climb steep brushy timber east through huckleberry and slide alder into meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide - loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points, and a rock rib - to the broad 6,480 ft saddle with running water and heather tent sites. Two days for most parties.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, for dry rock and a river crossing that is passable
hazards: a river crossing dependent on a cable car being in service
the Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
steep brushy timber, slide alder, and a loose divide traverse
rockfall and icefall from the glacier remnant in the couloir
a deep moat at the toe of the buttress late in the season
sustained hard climbing days from the nearest road, with a descent onto the other side of the peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Direct starts at the very bottom of the rock, and that is what separates it from the route it shares a camp with. From the saddle you first go down: steep scree trending climber's right, across several minor gullies, to the small glacier remnant filling the couloir below the wall.

The toe of the buttress lies on the right-hand side of that ice, where the rock runs down into the snow. That junction is the start. You should be tying in with the whole buttress rising above you and no snow left to climb.

The negative marker is unambiguous and it is the common mistake: the regular North Buttress walks past this toe and continues up the glacier on the buttress's climber's-left side, then moves onto slabs leading into a corner system well above the bottom of the rock. If you are still walking on snow with the buttress rising to your right, you have walked past the Direct and are heading for the regular start. Turn round and go back to where rock meets ice.

A second check is how soon it gets hard. The Direct gives sustained climbing from low down, with an offwidth, thin cracks and steep crest pitches; the regular line gives a snow climb and slabs first. A long easy start means you are not on the Direct.

Watch the moat at the junction. Where the neve has pulled away from the rock the gap deepens through the season and can be the hardest move of the day before any climbing has started.

approach_variants.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
approach_variants.notes: A much shorter walk to the same saddle camp exists from the road on the Canadian side, but it crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, which this page cannot say is lawful, and follows an unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread after the first stretch. It is the natural choice for parties already north of the border and the awkward one for parties starting south of it.
approach_variants.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
hazards: an international border crossing on foot
overgrown unmaintained tread
the same glacier remnant, moat and rockfall beneath the buttress
a cross-border rescue picture
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Arrival differs, the start does not. From the 6,480 ft saddle drop down steep scree trending climber's right, cross the minor gullies, and reach the glacier remnant under the couloir.

Tie in at the toe of the rock on the right-hand side of the ice, where the buttress runs down into the snow and there is no more snow above you. If you find yourself climbing neve with the buttress on your right, you have passed the Direct's start and are on the regular route's line toward the slabs and corner.

Expect the moat where snow has pulled back from the rock to be the first real obstacle, and expect the climbing to be hard immediately rather than after a snow lead.

approach_variants.name: Denny Creek Trail to Hemlock Pass, then the ridge
approach_variants.notes: The standard summer approach. From the Denny Creek trailhead (~2,300 ft), reached from I-90 Exit 47 by Denny Creek Road and FR 5830, follow the Denny Creek Trail #1014 toward Melakwa Lake past waterfalls and up steeper switchbacks to Hemlock Pass, about 4 miles and roughly 2,300 ft of gain. Leave the trail at the pass for the ridge on the right.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September for a dry scramble; earlier the ridge and talus hold snow and an axe is needed
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall on the summit block
Lingering snow on the ridge and talus early in the season
Brush in the notch below the talus once the snow has gone
Exposure on the north side of the summit block
approach_variants.baseFinding: Hemlock Pass is where the trail stops climbing. At its crest, before the trail drops toward Melakwa Lake, turn right onto the ridge and hold a bearing of about 33°, skirting the cliff bands mainly on their left. The check that you are on line is a plateau and meadow on the ridge, then a talus field wrapping most of the peak's base with the summit block above. Negative marker: if you are descending toward a lake, you stayed on the trail past the pass.

approach_variants.name: Alpental, Source Lake and Great Scott Basin to the Bryant-Chair gully
approach_variants.notes: A steeper alternative from the Alpental side, better known as a winter and spring snow climb than as a summer scramble. From the Alpental day-use trailhead at about 3,120 ft, take the Snow Lake Trail #1013 through old avalanche brush and second growth. At roughly 1.8 miles and 720 ft of gain, a boot path splits left (southwest) toward Source Lake while the main trail continues right toward Snow Lake Col. Drop briefly to cross Source Lake's outlet creek — the last dependable water — and follow the use trail along the lake's north and east shore into the open basin below The Tooth and Chair Peak. From there the tread becomes intermittent boot-track over boulders and heather benches, climbing southwest into Great Scott Basin under The Tooth's east face. Contour left (south) beneath the broken cliff bands on Bryant's east side and cross a talus field to the foot of the gully.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July to September once the gully has melted out; earlier the gully holds snow and needs an axe and crampons
hazards: The gully is an active avalanche path in winter and spring; avoid it in unstable snow or soon after a storm
Loose scree, with the centre and left of the gully markedly worse than the right
The gully funnels rockfall from parties above
Lingering early-season snow, requiring axe and crampons
Exposed and loose class 3 on the north side of the summit block when the block is dry
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The thumbtack is the landmark you walk past, and the gully is the one immediately beyond it. Contouring south beneath Bryant's east side you cross a talus field below the rock spire known locally as the Thumbtack. The mouth of the route's gully is at the far side of that talus. Spire behind you, steep scree-and-talus gully splitting the face in front of you.

What the gully is, in other words: this is the same drainage backcountry skiers call the Bryant Couloir or the wonder gully. If your winter partner knows the ski line, they know the route.

The footing test tells you where to be within it: climb favouring the far climbers' right side of the gully, which is noticeably firmer than the loose centre and left. A party grinding up loose ground in the middle is in the correct gully and in the wrong part of it.

Where it delivers you: the gully tops out on the Bryant-Chair connecting ridge, not on a summit. From there you work south over blocky ridge and talus to the base of the summit block. A gully that finishes on a summit is not this one.

And the last step changes character with the snow, which is worth knowing before you commit: with snow on the block the final scramble is easy class 3 with little real exposure. Dry, the only reasonable line goes round the north — climbers' left — side on exposed and distinctly loose class 3. Test every hold.

approach_variants.name: Snow Lakes trail to Perfection Lake, Prusik Pass and the Druid Plateau
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Snow Lakes trailhead, about four miles up Icicle Creek Road from Leavenworth. Follow Snow Lakes Trail #1553 through burn-scarred forest and switchbacks above Icicle Creek, past Nada and Snow Lakes at roughly six to seven miles, and on into the core basin — Lake Viviane, Leprechaun, Sprite, then Perfection Lake, by which point you have covered ten or eleven miles and about 6,000 ft.

At the north side of Perfection Lake, leave the main trail on the scramblers' path that switchbacks up to Prusik Pass at about 7,460-7,500 ft. That junction is easy to miss and the pass is the last reliable water.

From the pass everything is cross-country. Contour northwest across talus and heather benches at roughly 7,300-7,400 ft, keeping to the west side of the Lorelei Lakelets, then north to a broad rib at about 7,900-8,000 ft. From just below 8,000 ft turn northwest and climb steep talus and scree onto the Druid Plateau at about 8,350 ft.

There are no cairns and no tread above Prusik Pass. Round trip is 30-plus miles with 7,300-plus ft of gain, so essentially everyone camps.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the cross-country section above Prusik Pass frequently holds snow into July
hazards: No cairns and no tread above Prusik Pass — serious route-finding on talus and heather
Snow frequently lingering on the cross-country section into July
An exposed, holdless friction slab for the final fifteen feet, harder to downclimb than to climb
Verglas on shaded ground into July, adding real exposure to otherwise easy terrain
No bail-out shelter: sun, lightning and afternoon storms on open high ground
Core Zone overnight permits are competitive and effectively required
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The summit block is a separate object and the plateau is not the top. This is the failure mode on Cannon: parties gain the Druid Plateau at about 8,350 ft, find themselves on broad high ground, and treat arriving there as arriving. The actual climbing is a distinct block that only comes into view once you are on the plateau, across it to the west.

So the test is: can you see a discrete block of rock standing above the plateau surface? If you are on flat or gently rolling ground with nothing obviously above you, you have not crossed the plateau yet. Cross it and take the western slopes to the foot of the block.

Which side of the block, and this is the part that matters in cloud: the way up is a ramp on the block's south side. It is the last fifteen feet or so to the true summit, low-angle friction slab with almost no positive holds. If you have walked round the block and found only steep unfriendly rock, you are on the wrong aspect — keep going round to the south.

What the right ground feels like: this is a friction problem, not a hold problem. Approach shoes with good rubber, or rock shoes, make a real difference, and the downclimb of the same ramp is the psychological crux of the day for most parties because low-angle slab is harder to read going down.

Staging check below the plateau: from Prusik Pass you should pass the Lorelei Lakelets on their west side and reach a broad rib around 7,900-8,000 ft before turning northwest. If you passed the lakelets on their east, you are drifting toward the wrong drainage.

approach_variants.name: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Cannon Creek basin — the shorter, rougher side
approach_variants.notes:
The documented alternative reaches the same staging ground near the Druid Plateau from the north instead, out of the Stuart Lake trailhead: up the Mountaineer Creek valley and then cross-country into the Cannon Creek basin.

This is much shorter than the Snow Lakes walk, and that is the whole of its appeal. It is also markedly rougher: the lower section is brushy and there are cliff bands to negotiate, and there is no trail for any of it.

Cannon has no maintained trail to its summit by any line, so both approaches end in the same cross-country problem. What differs is how much of the day is spent on tread before that starts — nearly all of it on the Snow Lakes side, very little on this one.

No reliable published time or distance exists for this variant and none is given. Treat it as a full day of navigation rather than a walk with a scramble at the end.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the lower cross-country section is brushy and holds snow later than the trail does
hazards: Brushy lower cross-country with cliff bands to negotiate and no trail
No cairns or tread anywhere on the upper mountain
An exposed holdless friction ramp on the summit block
Snow and verglas on shaded ground into July
No published timing for this variant — plan conservatively
No bail-out shelter on the high ground
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Both approaches converge on the Druid Plateau, so the base test is identical and the arrival test is not. Coming from the north you reach the plateau area from the Cannon Creek basin rather than from Prusik Pass, so the Lorelei Lakelets and the broad rib are not on your route and cannot be used to confirm position — do not try to apply the southern approach's landmarks here.

What still holds: the summit block is a distinct object standing above the plateau, reached across the plateau on its western slopes, and the way up it is a low-angle friction ramp on its south side, roughly the last fifteen feet to the true summit. Almost no positive holds. That is the base, and it is the same base for anyone who gets here.

The north-side-specific warning: the ground below the basin has cliff bands in it. Unlike the southern route, where the navigation problem is featureless open talus, here it is possible to be cliffed out and to have to lose height to get round. If you are on steepening ground with the basin still above you, come down and traverse rather than pushing on.

And a route-choice note: the northeast ridge is a separate line on this mountain and is described as an ascent route only, with most parties descending the Prusik Pass side. If you have come up from the north expecting to reverse it, check which line you are actually on before committing to that plan.

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek trail and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail
approach_variants.notes:
This is the way in that stays entirely inside the United States, and it is the reason the peak costs three or four days.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross the lake by water taxi, or paddle a private or inflatable boat portaged down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail starts at about 1,500 ft. Parties with their own boat commonly start walking around four in the morning to leave daylight for the day above; the water taxi runs only in the daytime, 8am to 5pm.

After a couple of hours watch for the junction with the old, no-longer-maintained Freezeout Creek trail. The stretch immediately above that junction is the hardest navigation of the entire approach: steep rock and alder slopes that want a rising, diagonal line before you regain forest and real tread. Intermittent orange flagging marks it and is worth hunting for.

Back in the trees the tread improves up to a cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited just after a creek crossing — bunks, a wood stove and a logbook, and a useful emergency shelter. About a quarter mile past it, cross the creek again and pass through an old burn. Tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

The lower part of this corridor is national recreation area and needs a park backcountry permit for camping; above the boundary it is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September in a normal year; the creek is hard to ford until the snowmelt drops
hazards: Several similar-looking gullies in the upper basin; the wrong one cliffs out above the creek
The steep rock-and-alder section above the trail junction is the hardest navigation of the approach
Krummholz and vegetation-covered rock on the crux band
Teetering blocks near the summit
Days long enough that parties routinely finish the descent in the dark, with a boat pickup to make
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no rock start to find on this route. What you are finding is the right gully out of a basin that offers several, and getting that wrong is how parties get cliffed out.

Above where the tread dies, climb the Freezeout drainage and work up steep heather, talus and scree toward the notch on the ridge at about 7,600 ft. That notch is the target and it is the only feature in the upper basin worth navigating to. Cross to the east side of the creek at roughly 5,000 ft on the way up.

The physical tests on the climb itself are rock quality and terrain grade, in that order. This is granite and the rock is genuinely good — clean, coarse and solid, the sort people compare to the best cragging ranges. It is mostly class 2 with short class 3 steps, and the crux is a steeper band with krummholz and bluffs where you are pulling on vegetation-covered rock. If you are roping up, you are off route.

The negative marker is enormous and unmistakable. This peak's north side is a fourteen-hundred-foot wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs holding ice or the remains of it, with a glacier at its foot. If you are looking up at that, you are on the wrong side of the mountain entirely and you are under the technical routes. The scramble never sees the north face.

Mark your exact ascent gully before you leave it, and this is the single most important sentence here. The upper basin holds several gullies and chutes that look alike from above, and dropping into the wrong one on descent risks cliffing out on bluffs well above the creek. Do not improvise a shortcut down. Reverse exactly what you came up.

Near the summit, watch teetering blocks, and expect the final ground to be exposed and windy.

approach_variants.name: The crest trail north from Harts Pass to Castle Pass
approach_variants.notes:
The third way in, and the one that trades a boat for a great deal of walking. The high pass road climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. It opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July, and closes with the first serious autumn storms.

From the pass, the crest trail runs north through country that starts near 6,200 ft and barely drops below 5,000 ft, over a high pass and on to Castle Pass, where it meets the Boundary Trail running east across the Pasayten and west toward the lake. Camps along the way are open and windy; pitch behind timber rather than in the meadow.

This stays inside the United States throughout, and it needs no boat.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the high road is open and the traverse is clear of snow
hazards: A long unpaved mountain road with 17 percent grades, no passing room and an unguarded drop
The road opens late and closes with the first autumn storms
Very long approach on foot with exposed, windy high camps
The international boundary lies about a mile north of the summit and crossing it here is unlawful
Similar-looking descent gullies that cliff out above the creek
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Castle Pass the peak lies roughly four miles to the west-northwest, and what you are looking for is the head of the drainage on its southern flank rather than a base of rock.

Drop off the pass into the head of the creek basin on the peak's south side and work up it. The scramble ground is the same ground the eastern approach reaches from the other direction: heather, talus and scree leading to the notch on the ridge at about 7,600 ft, then class 2 granite with short class 3 steps to the summit.

The confirming test is the rock. Once you are on it, the granite is clean, coarse and solid, and the difficulty stays at scrambling grade with one steeper krummholz-and-bluff band as the crux. Roped climbing means you are not on the standard route.

Negative marker, and it is the whole mountain: the north side is a fourteen-hundred-foot granite wall above a glacier. From anywhere on this approach you should be looking at broken scrambling ground, not at a wall. If a wall is above you, you have gone round the mountain.

Second negative marker, and it is a legal one rather than a navigational one. The summit sits about a mile south of the international boundary and the boundary clearing is visible from high on the peak. Do not follow ground north from the summit or from the basin. Crossing on foot away from a port of entry is not a lawful crossing, the corridor is patrolled, and this is the one mistake here that ends with more than a long walk.

On descent, mark your ascent gully. The basin holds several that look alike from above and the wrong one cliffs out.

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
approach_variants.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. This is the shortest drive of the three ways in and it is paved the whole way.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles cross an old burn, so there is almost no shade, the tread is overgrown and soaks you after rain, and blowdown is normal. Andrews Creek runs beside the trail for that whole stretch and is reliable water. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

From the pass continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Bear off near the old wilderness guard-station cabin. Strong parties walk it in one long day with heavy packs; others split it with a camp partway up the drainage.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking way in from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the penalties are severe.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-July through September, once the trails and the face have shed snow
hazards: No climbers' trail and no marked start; the base is identified by landform and by what is above you
Rockfall from parties above and from loose blocks on the featured lower face
Afternoon storms on a summit that is the local high point
A walk-off descent whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap near the summit
Remote enough that any injury becomes a multi-day evacuation
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no climbers' trail to the base. Cross the parkland and talus from camp toward the deep gully that divides Cathedral Peak from The Monk, the semi-detached tower leaning against the lower right side of the wall. Thirty to sixty minutes from camp.

The first test is the tower, and it is a negative one. This route is on the main wall, not on the tower and not on the buttress behind it. If a separate tower stands between you and the rock you are about to climb, walk further left along the base — you are under the Southeast Buttress. If you are looking up at an open thousand-foot face with nothing standing in front of it, you are in the right place.

Now place yourself across that face. This line takes the right-hand portion of the open wall, between the central line and the line further right. There is no start ledge, no cairn and no fixed gear to find; the ground low down is heavily featured and the first ascent treated it as choose-your-own, so the start is a zone rather than a point. Pick the most featured rock in that right-hand third and go up.

Confirm it above you before you commit, because the low ground will accept almost any line. Look for a long ramp slashing rightward across the middle of the face, and above the ramp a steep, clean crack splitting a headwall. Those two features in that order are this route. If the ramp is not there and instead you find a big curving chimney above you, you have drifted into the centre of the wall and you are on the original central line — several number grades easier, and a different day.

Second negative marker, at the top: this route joins the buttress route for its final hand crack to the summit. Arriving at that shared pitch is correct. Arriving at it early, without having crossed a rightward ramp and pulled a thin headwall, means you traversed off.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
approach_variants.notes:
This is a trail, #510A, not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then the forest roads up to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print under three or four spellings, and one of those names also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not to the name.

The trail descends from its high trailhead to join the valley trail below, and from there it is the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. This is the shortest walk and the least climbing of the ways in.

The catch sits at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail drops to meet the valley, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out, at the point when you least want it.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-July through September
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip, on the way out
A trailhead published under several different names
Same lack of any climbers' trail to the base
Beta headed South Face may describe the small tower rather than the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The way in changes; the base does not. From Upper Cathedral Lake it is the same walk toward the deep gully dividing Cathedral Peak from The Monk, and the same question at the bottom: is there a tower standing between you and the rock? If yes you are under the buttress, not this face.

What this approach genuinely changes is your first sighting of the wall. Coming up the valley you arrive in the basin from below rather than over the pass, so the whole south side presents itself at once from across the water. Use that. Standing at the lake, pick out three things before you walk up: the tower at the lower right of the wall, the open thousand-foot face left of it, and the long ramp that slashes rightward across the middle of that face. This route is the right-hand third of the open face, working up to that ramp and to the steep crack in the headwall above it.

That identification is far easier from across the lake than from underneath, where the face foreshortens and the ramp disappears into the general featuring. Photograph it or draw it before you leave camp.

Negative marker: if from the lake you cannot see a ramp at all on the face you are looking at, you are looking at the wrong wall. The tower has its own south face with its own short routes on it, and beta written about that tower will also say South Face. The tower is small and stands clear of the mountain; the main face runs the full height of the peak behind it.

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
approach_variants.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,080 ft, roughly a five-hour drive from Seattle and the shortest drive of the three ways in.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles pass through an old burn, so there is little shade and the tread can be overgrown and wet after rain, but the creek is beside you and reliable. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

Continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Published figures for the whole walk from this trailhead are about nineteen miles with 5,550 ft of gain, and everyone splits it over at least two days.

Of the three trailheads this one has the shortest drive and the most walking gain; the Thirtymile trailhead is only about five and a half miles further along the same road, which makes a car shuttle between them easy.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking approach from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the fines are severe.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow lingers at Andrews Pass into early July
hazards: No climbers' trail to the base; navigation is off the landform and photographs
Long approach through burn with little shade and overgrown tread
A no-fall step-across or hop on the walk-off descent
Remote enough that a two- to four-day trip is the norm, so a retreat is slow
approach_variants.baseFinding: There is no climbers' trail to the base. A party who got there reported finding none and navigating purely off photographs, so stop looking for tread and navigate by the landform. The landform is the deep gully that separates Cathedral Peak from The Monk, the semi-detached tower on the lower right side of the south face. One published account leaves the maintained trail at the first switchback after Cathedral Pass and heads for the gully from there; others come across the parkland between Upper Cathedral Lake and the pass. Both end up in the same place, thirty to sixty minutes from camp. Go up into the gully — do not stop at its mouth. Three accounts put the start of the first pitch about 150 feet up the Cathedral–Monk gully, on the left wall, which is the Cathedral side. Scramble onto a tall pedestal there; it gives a decent belay stance to start from. Pedestal, left wall, about 150 feet in: that is the whole identification. How to tell this from the South Face routes, and it is a simple physical test: is there a semi-detached tower standing between you and the wall? If yes, you are at the SE Buttress, which follows the ridge behind The Monk on the right-hand edge of the south face. If you are walking up to an open face with nothing in front of it, that is the South Face route, a different and much harder climb. A related trap in the naming rather than on the ground: The Monk has its own south face with its own routes on it. Beta headed South Face may be describing the tower, not the mountain. Coming down, the descent is the walk-off to the west and then south-west back toward Upper Cathedral Lake, and its crux is a gap the route description tells you to hop across. It can be avoided by downclimbing the exposed nose beside it and stepping over — easy when dry, but no-fall ground.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
approach_variants.notes:
This is a trail, #510A, and not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to the Iron Gate spur, a different road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then NF-39 and NF-300 to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print as Cathedral Driveway, Chewuch, and Chewack Driveway, and the Chewuch name also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not the name.

The Cathedral Driveway descends from its trailhead to join the Chewuch trail #510 around mile 4.8 at about 4,300 ft, and from there it is the Chewuch valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. Total is about seventeen and a half miles with roughly 3,700 ft of gain — the shortest walk and the least climbing of the three approaches.

The catch is at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead sits high and the trail drops to meet the Chewuch, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out, at the point when you least want it.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip on the way out
A trailhead with four different published names
Same lack of any climbers' trail to the base
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The approach changes but the base does not. From camp at Upper Cathedral Lake it is the same thirty to sixty minutes: cross toward the deep gully dividing Cathedral Peak from The Monk, go about 150 feet up into the gully, and start on the left wall from a tall pedestal.

What this approach does affect is your first sighting. Coming down the Chewuch you arrive in the basin from below rather than over Andrews Pass, so take the time at the lake to pick out The Monk as a separate tower leaning against the peak's flank before walking up. The tower in front of the wall is the whole discriminator between this route and the South Face, and it is far easier to identify from across the water than from underneath.

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 to Upper Cathedral Lake, then the trail toward Cathedral Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft and walk trail #504 up the drainage to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft. The lower half is an old burn with no shade and brushy tread. From the pass, drop into the next drainage and take the Cathedral Lakes trail up to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. That is the base camp and it is a full long day of walking, usually two.

One early-season bonus is worth planning around: the chasm that splits the summit rocks is often snow-filled early, which makes the first step-across easy or trivial. Late season means a bare hole and the pure version of the move. It can snow here in any month, so carry layers whatever the forecast says.

The alternatives are the valley trail from the Thirtymile trailhead, gentle but longer, and the Cathedral Driveway trail from the high trailhead above Loomis (not the longer Iron Gate route), which walks least but drives longest and leaves you 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
approach_variants.season: July to mid-September; the sunny south-west aspect melts out first
hazards: The step-across onto the chockstone is easy climbing over serious exposure and is harder in descent than in ascent
The second step-across never has snow in the hole, whatever the season
Ducks and cairns are the only route markers on the granite section
Loose blocks and sandy slopes that plunge-step well going down and slide going up
This is also the descent for every technical route here, so parties meet it tired and often late in the day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route has no rock start to find. It begins where you leave the trail, and that spot is defined by the pass, not by a cairn: walk about 0.6 mile of trail from Upper Cathedral Lake toward Cathedral Pass and step off just short of the pass at roughly 7,600 ft. If you have crested the pass and started descending the far side, you have gone too far — turn round.

Above that, the route confirms itself by texture, in a fixed order. First several hundred vertical feet of easy sandy slopes with no rock scrambling at all. Then ducks and cairns over coarse granite blocks and slabs, solid rock, class 2 to 3, with two minor steps that need a hand and one place where a friction push gets you over a block. If you are pulling on anything harder than that, you have wandered off the ducks.

The route then enters a hidden cleft running parallel to and just below the west ridge crest. That cleft is the strongest confirmation on the whole climb, because it cannot be seen from below and you either find yourself in it or you do not.

The last feature is the crux and it is unmistakable: a long chasm cleaving the summit rocks into a north and a south half, with a big chockstone jammed in the slot. Step onto the chockstone and mantle onto the bulge on the far side. The move is easy; the exposure is not, and most parties rig a handline with prusiks for the return. Lower down there is a cannonhole giving an easier alternative to one vertical step.

Negative marker: if at any point you are standing under a thousand-foot wall with a detached tower leaning against its lower right side, you have walked round to the south side of the mountain and you are below the technical routes, not on the walk-up.

approach_variants.name: Upper Cathedral Lake camp, then the grassy south-east slope onto the ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Reach Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft by any of the long trails — Andrews Creek #504 is the shortest drive, the Cathedral Driveway #510A the shortest walk, Thirtymile via the Chewuch #510 the middle option. All are multi-day and all put you in the same basin.

From the Boundary Trail below the peak, this route does not go into the Cathedral–Monk gully at all. Scramble up the grassy south-east slope directly from the main trail to gain the ridge.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Continuing north along the ridge toward The Pope and the Canadian border
Loose rock on a long broken ridge
Very long walk out from a remote basin if anything goes wrong
A no-fall step-across on the standard walk-off descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are aiming for the long broken ridge that runs between Cathedral Peak and The Pope, a separate small peak further north along the same crest, sitting right on the Canada–United States border.

That relationship is the base-finding and it is also the warning. The ridge has a peak at each end. If you keep working north along the crest past the point where the ground starts descending away from Cathedral, you are heading for The Pope and, shortly after that, for an international border it is illegal to cross here.

The route itself confirms as you go rather than at a single spot: each pitch has a move or two of old-school 5.3 with scrambling between, so seven pitches of mostly-easy ground with occasional short difficulties is correct here and is not a sign you have wandered onto the walk-up. The real crux announces itself — about 400 feet below the summit you cross a dike, and the two short pitches immediately above that dike are the hardest climbing on the route. A final airy fourth-class scramble finishes it.

Negative marker for the start: if you find yourself entering a deep gully with a detached tower on your right, you have walked to the SE Buttress start. The NE Ridge is gained from open grassy slope off the main trail, with no gully involved.

Descent is the ordinary walk-up route to the west, and a short rappel may be wanted to get off the summit ridge.

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
approach_variants.notes:
The drive is the easy part — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. The walk is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state.

Trail #504 climbs the drainage for roughly twelve miles to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, crossing an old burn for much of that: hot, rocky, buggy, and no shade. From the pass the trail drops into the next drainage before the Cathedral Lakes side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft, below the peak's south-west side.

Treat this as a two-to-four day backpack with a summit push from camp in the basin. A free self-issue wilderness permit is taken at the trailhead along with a parking pass. There is no cell coverage anywhere on this trip.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
hazards: Three separate routes share this face and the lower ground accepts almost any line
The tower in front of the wall carries its own routes under a colliding name
Loose rock and rockfall from parties above on a wall this size
Walk-off descent to the west whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap
No cell coverage and a multi-day walk out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From camp, follow the trail toward Cathedral Pass and then climb scree and talus to the foot of the main wall. Thirty to sixty minutes.

First, rule out the tower. A semi-detached tower leans against the lower right side of the wall, and a deep gully separates it from the mountain. If that tower is between you and the rock, you are under the buttress route, which climbs the ridge behind it. This route is on the open wall, and specifically on its centre. Nothing should be standing in front of you.

Start low and central, near the bottom of the wall rather than off to one side. The line then confirms itself by a run of features in a fixed order, and this is the identification that actually works, because the lower face accepts many lines:

Low down there is a boxed-in feature the first ascent called a confession box. At mid-height there is a spectacular curving chimney — this is the single best confirmation on the route and it is visible from the ground if you look for it. High up you cross a pulpit ledge and then a belfry ledge before easier ground runs to the top.

Negative marker, and it matters because the two lines converge: if instead of a curving chimney you find yourself pushed rightward along a long ramp toward a steep thin crack in a headwall, you have drifted onto the harder line that takes the right-hand third of the face. That one is several number grades above this and it takes very thin protection. Come back left and look for the chimney.

Second negative marker: the tower in front of the wall has its own small south face carrying several short routes. Beta written about the tower will also be headed South Face. The tower's routes are two to five pitches; this wall is about a thousand feet.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
approach_variants.notes:
The high trailhead above Loomis, reached by Toats Coulee Road and the forest roads beyond it, sits at about 5,570 ft. This is a trail and not a four-wheel-drive road, whatever you may have read; the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur.

The trail drops from the trailhead to meet the valley trail lower down, then follows the valley up to the Cathedral Lakes basin. It is the shortest walk and the least total climbing of the ways in.

Both ends carry a penalty. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail loses height to reach the valley, the trip finishes with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip on the way out
A trailhead published under several different names
The wall foreshortens badly from directly below, so the mid-height chimney is hard to relocate at the base
Same walk-off descent with a no-fall gap crossing near the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the same and reached the same way from camp. What changes is where you first see the wall, and on a face this size that is worth more than any description.

Coming up the valley you enter the basin from below rather than over the pass, so the whole south side stands up in front of you at once. Stop at the lake and sort out three things before walking up: the small detached tower at the lower right of the wall; the deep gully between that tower and the mountain; and the open centre of the wall to the left of both. This route is the open centre.

While you are looking, find the curving chimney at mid-height in that centre panel. It is the feature that proves the line and it is far easier to pick out from across the water than from underneath, where the wall foreshortens and everything reads as featured granite. Fix it against the skyline above it so you can re-find it at the base.

Negative marker from the lake: if the panel you are looking at has a long ramp cutting rightward across it toward a steep headwall crack, that is the right-hand line, not this one. And if the wall you are looking at is only a few pitches tall and stands clear of the mountain, you are looking at the tower.

approach_variants.name: PCT from Snoqualmie Pass, leaving the trail half a mile short of Chikamin Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead, Trail #2000, off I-90 exit 52, the trail switchbacks through timber and avalanche paths, crosses beneath Kendall Peak, and reaches the Kendall Katwalk around mile 5 at about 5,400 ft — a good checkpoint, though not reliable water late in the season.

Continue north past Ridge Lake at about mile 6.5, which has reliable camping and water, and the Alaska Lake and Joe Lake junctions, then along the rolling rocky PCT beneath Alaska and Huckleberry Mountains to the Huckleberry-Chikamin saddle around mile 10.25. The trail then contours below the Four Brothers and Chikamin's south face, passing the Park Lakes Trail junction.

About 13.5 miles one way to the base of the gullies with roughly 4,600 ft of gain, so most parties camp at Ridge Lake or the 5,200 ft pack camp and make it a two or three day trip.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: An unmarked gully turnoff near Chikamin Pass — overshooting puts you in the cliffy Four Brothers
Loose scree and rockfall in the upper gully system
A steep, snow-filled and rubble-choked gully in early season
Short but exposed class 3 moves on the summit horn
A long trail approach with camps well short of the peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The test is to leave the trail before you reach the pass, and that is counter-intuitive enough that it is the whole finding. At roughly mile 13.5 — about half a mile short of Chikamin Pass, near an established pack camp at about 5,200 ft — leave the PCT and climb steep grassy and heather slopes into the gully systems on the south and southeast face.

The negative is explicit and expensive: do not continue to Chikamin Pass before cutting uphill. Doing so puts you in the middle of the Four Brothers, a band of cliffy towers that force technical terrain on a route that is otherwise a scramble. If you are standing at Chikamin Pass, you have overshot the turn.

So use the pack camp as the marker: an established camp at about 5,200 ft on the trail, with the peak's south face above and the pass still ahead of you. Turn uphill there.

What the ground should do, in order: class 2 hiking low on grass and heather, then loose scree and dirt-and-heather slots in the upper gully, sustained class 3 as you gain Chikamin Ridge with some exposure near the crest, and finally a short, well-protected class 3-4 chimney or slot of about 10 ft right below the summit block, with roughly 75 more feet of easy scrambling above it to the top. A 10 ft chimney immediately below the summit horn is the confirming feature.

Snow changes the character of the gully entirely: early in the season it is a steep, rubble-choked chute and an axe is needed.

approach_variants.name: Mineral Creek and Park Lakes, then the gullies above Glacier Lake
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mineral Creek trailhead, Trail #1331, at the end of FR-46 / Cooper Pass Road at about 2,400 ft, the trail is brushy low down but well trodden. It climbs steadily beside Mineral Creek to Park Lakes at 4.3 to 5.4 miles and about 2,570 ft of gain, and ties into the PCT.

From the PCT / Park Lakes junction, head north toward the Spectacle Point saddle overlooking Spectacle Lake, then drop about a mile to Glacier Lake, a common camp, before climbing the southeast-slope gullies above it.

This is the shortest line in — day-trip feasible for a strong party at roughly 14 to 16.5 miles round trip — but the tread is rougher and there are creek crossings low down.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: Brushy lower trail and creek crossings on the Mineral Creek approach
Loose scree and rockfall in the upper gullies
Exposure near the final ridge crest
Snow-filled gullies in early season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From this side the arrival is a lake, not a trail junction: you climb the gullies directly above Glacier Lake. Standing at the lake with the southeast slopes rising in front of you is the arrival, and the lake is a hard landmark that cloud does not remove.

What the ground below the gullies looks like, as confirmation: brooks, waterfalls, tarns, heather benches, sandstone slabs and blocky breccia low down. Running water and heather benches are right for this side; if you are on bare scree from the lake upward, you have started too high.

The two approaches meet on the same upper mountain, so the finding from there is identical: loose scree and dirt-and-heather slots in the upper gully, sustained class 3 to the crest of Chikamin Ridge, and a short well-protected 10 ft class 3-4 chimney below the summit block with about 75 ft of easy scrambling above it.

And the same negative applies once you are on the PCT: do not wander south toward Chikamin Pass looking for a way up. The Four Brothers sit between the pass and the route.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Spider Gap (standard)
approach_variants.notes: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (~3,500 ft), Trail #1511 climbs the valley about 6.5 miles to Spider Meadows, then into upper Phelps Basin and up the Spider Glacier snowfield to Spider Gap at 7,100 ft. Descend the north side — the steepest 100 vertical feet first, softer snow tends to be climber's-left — then scree and easing snowfield past the Lyman Glacier to Lower Lyman Lake, and back up about 1.8 miles of open meadow to Cloudy Pass at 6,438 ft. This is the line the recorded distance matches.
approach_variants.season: Jul–Sep
hazards: Spider Gap is the crux of the approach — a permanent snow/glacier slope that is a straightforward boot-pack in summer but can hold open crevasses and firm icy snow early season. Carry an axe and know how to use it.
A whiteout or an early-morning refreeze moves crampons from optional to necessary.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cloudy Pass is the staging point, not the base: the climbing starts where the boot path leaves the meadows and gains the southwest ridge, with the summit about 1,500 ft above the pass.

approach_variants.name: Buck Creek Trail from Trinity, over Buck Creek Pass
approach_variants.notes: A longer alternative reaching Cloudy Pass from the Trinity Trailhead by way of Buck Creek Pass. One of the three ways in; it is a multi-day trip rather than a variation on the standard day.
approach_variants.season: Jul–Sep

approach_variants.name: Railroad Creek from Holden Village
approach_variants.notes: Reaches Lower Lyman Lake and Cloudy Pass from Holden Village, which is itself reached by the Lake Chelan boat and a vehicle shuttle. The longest of the three and the one with the most fixed logistics.
approach_variants.season: Jul–Sep

approach_variants.name: The SR-20 South Buttress pullout, then bear right into the basin beneath the North Ridge Notch
approach_variants.notes:
The standard approach uses the same SR-20 pullout as the South Buttress, on the north side of the highway about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass. Follow the South Buttress approach: creek crossing, brushy climbers' path into the meadow, up into the boulder field.

Eight pitches at 5.7. It sees far less traffic than the South Buttress, the peak's classic line.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A loose, runout 5.7 PG13 pitch with marginal protection simply to reach the base of the ridge
A descent that leaves the ridge at the notch and continues down a different route's rappel line
Loose rock and brush on the lower approach
A more direct West Ridge descent from higher on the North Ridge exists but is considered worse for rockfall
approach_variants.baseFinding:
At the boulder field, bear right and north into the basin beneath the north ridge notch, rather than left toward the south buttress gully. That is the fork, and left versus right is the whole difference between two of this peak's routes.

The route's real base is the notch, and getting to it is itself a pitch: from the basin, A loose, runout 5.7 PG13 pitch gains the north ridge notch. Protection is marginal, one or two small cams and narrow-head-width pieces help, and this pitch should be treated as the technical and psychological crux of the approach, not of the ridge above it.

So the test is blunt: if the hardest, scariest thing you have done is the pitch that got you to the notch, you are on the right route. If you got to a notch by walking, you are somewhere else.

Arrival: a notch, a gap on the crest with the ridge running above it. Everything above is the North Ridge.

The northern alternative, which arrives at the same notch from the other side: from Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail into the Porcupine Creek drainage, then climb two or three short pitches of low fifth class to gain the North Ridge Notch from that side. That is a legitimate option for parties camping near Rainy Pass, and it adds significant approach time. Two or three easy pitches versus one hard runout one is how you tell which side you came up.

Descent does not reverse the approach pitch all the way: from the summit, reverse the North Ridge with several short rappels through the steeper fifth-class steps, then one longer rappel back into the North Ridge Notch. From the notch, descend via the standard South Buttress and West Ridge line, downclimbing to the first set of bolted chain rappel anchors and continuing down the same four-rappel West Ridge sequence, a single 60 m rope sufficient for each, before the final scramble through the scree bowl and boulder field back to the meadow and creek crossing.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, via the South Buttress climbers' trail

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek route
approach_variants.notes:
From the Suiattle River Road, take the Downey Creek Trail on the east bank through old growth — about six and a half miles to the Six Mile campsite at roughly 2,440 ft. The maintained trail effectively ends there.

The Bachelor Creek route continues on the north side of the creek and crosses to the south at about 4,000 ft on a log; some parties cross higher, nearer 4,400. Between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft the tread is genuinely overgrown — parties describe swimming through brush without being able to see their feet — but the important point is that the trail IS still there under it, so do not abandon it and start making your own line. At about 4,500 ft an old avalanche swath from 2002 wiped out the trail and this is the hardest stretch to get through.

Above that, cross the pass at about 5,900 ft north-west of Cub Lake and descend to the lake at 5,338 ft, around fourteen miles in. Good camping. A well-established trail then crosses flats and climbs heather beside a cascade to Itswoot Ridge at about 6,200 ft, which is the better-placed camp for summit day. Reported car-to-camp times have been nine to eleven hours; this is a multi-day approach, not a hike-in.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: brush so dense between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft that the trail is invisible underfoot
the 2002 avalanche swath at about 4,500 ft where the trail is destroyed
Bachelor Creek crossing on a log
open avalanche paths below Spire Point in early-season snow
crevasses on the Dome Glacier
unmarked cross-country traverse if the cairns are lost
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Itswoot Ridge the traverse north-east toward the Dome Glacier goes through a basin that is well marked with cairns and is followable even with reduced visibility — so in cloud, look for cairns rather than trying to hold a bearing. Losing the cairns is the sign you have drifted.

The climbing starts where you rope up at the glacier's edge. The upper Dome Glacier is mellow, so the arrival is undramatic; the feature you are climbing to is the notch or col at 8,560 ft immediately north of the summit block. It is confirmed by what happens on the far side: from the col a snow slope of about three hundred feet and then a rock arete of about five hundred feet lead to the summit at 8,920 ft.

The useful cross-check in poor visibility is that the col also gives onto the Chickamin Glacier beyond — a much larger icefield than the one you came up. So a very big glacier appearing on the far side is correct and not a sign you are in the wrong place; the thing to verify is that the summit block is immediately to your south. If the ground on the far side does not drop away onto a large icefield, you are at a different notch.

approach_variants.name: Ptarmigan Traverse from Cascade Pass
approach_variants.notes: Dome Peak is the far end of the Ptarmigan Traverse, so it is also reached from the Cascade Pass trailhead by travelling the whole traverse south. This is the long way in by a wide margin and is undertaken as part of the traverse rather than as an approach to the peak; parties heading only for Dome use the Downey Creek side.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: multi-day committing traverse with several glacier crossings before Dome is reached
crevasses on the Dome Glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding: Arriving from the north along the traverse, the reference points are the same: the cairned basin traverse toward the Dome Glacier, and the 8,560 ft col north of the summit block with the Chickamin Glacier beyond it and the summit rock arete immediately to the south.

approach_variants.name: Bacon-Hagan saddle and the southwest couloir
approach_variants.notes: This is the line used by parties arriving on the traverse from the Watson and Bacon side: descend north off the glacier and past several tarns, then follow a heathered ridge to the saddle between Hagan Mountain and Bacon Peak, where a small tarn sits with reliable water. From the tarn, bushwhack north up steep forest, working through two distinct rock cliffbands — the sustained route-finding crux of the whole approach — picking brushy ramps and weaknesses through each band to keep the ground climbable. Above them the timber breaks out onto open heather and grass on Hagan's south flank around 6,000 to 6,400 ft, with seasonal snowmelt water and rough camps. Mark your line through the cliffbands with photos, cairns or a track before going higher: the weaknesses you threaded are hard to spot from above, and the descent is consistently slower and more error-prone than the climb.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Two cliffbands in steep timber with no marked line through them
Loose rock the whole length of the scree-and-talus couloir — helmets, and a tight party
Crevasses and moats on the Hagan Glacier ice apron even in summer
The descent reverses ground that reads very differently from above
approach_variants.baseFinding: A broad scree-and-talus couloir, topping out at a col at the southwest end of the crags. From the open heather and grass benches on Hagan's south flank, one broad couloir of loose scree and talus leads up to a col near the southwest end of the line of Hagan summit crags, around 7,000 ft. That col is the base of the climbing, and the slabs above it on the south side go at Class 3 to the top. Hagan is a massif of several crags rather than a single peak, so which col you reach matters: if the notch you have gained sits in the middle of the crags with towers rising on both sides of you, it is not this one — keep working to the southwest end of the line. Note carefully where the couloir meets the heather benches before you leave them, because it is also the way down and it is far harder to identify from above.

approach_variants.name: Lower Blum Lake and the 6,831 ft pass
approach_variants.notes: The approach from the north, out of the Blum Lakes basin rather than off the Bacon side. From lower Blum Lake, traverse south and rope up for glacier travel to a pass at 6,831 ft that sits between the south and middle Hagan peaks. This is glacier ground and the rope goes on before the traverse, not at the pass. Parties reaching the Blum Lakes come up the climbers' path off the Baker River Trail near Blum Creek, a faint path in brush marked with flagging tape that climbs the ridge to about 4,000 ft before veering south and traversing toward the lakes.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Glacier travel with crevasse hazard between lower Blum Lake and the pass
The Blum climbers' path is faint, brushy and marked only with flagging tape
Loose rock and exposure on the spur and summit ridge above the notch
Several named crags on one massif — easy to commit to the wrong summit
approach_variants.baseFinding: The pass sits between the south and middle peaks, and it is the south peak you climb. Arriving at 6,831 ft, you should have a summit on either hand: this is a pass between two of Hagan's own peaks, not a col on the outside of the massif, and if only one side of you rises to rock you are in the wrong gap. The climbing then goes up the south peak's north side to a notch on its upper east side — that notch is high on the peak, not at the pass, and it is on the east flank, so a notch you can walk into from the west is the wrong one. From the notch, traverse onto the south face and gain the summit ridge, work up a spur on the east, then bear around to the south, where slabs lead to the summit at Class 3. The finish is south-facing slab, not a gully: if you are grovelling up a loose gully at the top you have missed the traverse around to the south side.

approach_variants.name: East Bank Trail on foot from milepost 138, leaving it at May Creek
approach_variants.notes: Park at the East Bank Trailhead near milepost 138 at about 1,800 ft. The trail drops immediately to the bridge over Ruby Creek and then runs north along Ross Lake, mostly flat and fast, to the May Creek camp. This is the whole of the easy walking. At May Creek leave the trail and climb west to north-west, staying loosely between the creeks on the mountain's west side. Cliff bands start around 3,200 ft and are threaded on boot and game trails rather than climbed; snow generally begins around 4,800 to 5,000 ft. Three miles or so of that work reaches a flat camp just over 5,200 ft below the toe of the ice. Strong parties carry a second camp onto the upper glacier near 7,400 ft, which shortens summit day considerably.
approach_variants.season: Late May through July while the headwall is still a snow climb; the highway gate closes the season at both ends
hazards: steep brushy timber with cliff bands from about 3,200 ft, far worse to reverse than to ascend
crevasses on the Nohokomeen Glacier, thinly bridged late in the season
sustained steep snow on the headwall itself, with a long runout onto the glacier below
rockfall and icefall off the wall once the sun reaches it
a two to four day commitment with no quick way off the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The timber belt is the navigation, the glacier toe is the arrival. Leaving May Creek you are looking for weaknesses, not a line: the cliff bands from about 3,200 ft up are passed on boot and game trails that thread left and right, so a section that forces you to climb rock means you have pushed into the band rather than around it. The reliable signal that you are through is underfoot rather than overhead - continuous snow starting somewhere near 4,800 to 5,000 ft, and above that the timber gives out onto open ground.

The camp is a flat bench, not a viewpoint. Just over 5,200 ft the ground levels into a flat bench directly below the toe of the ice. If you are on sloping heather with the ice still out of sight above you, keep going; if you are already on the ice you have walked past the bench.

The headwall is above the glacier, not at its toe. From the bench the glacier runs up in front of you at an easy angle for a long way before anything steepens. The route's steep ground is the wall at the head of that ice, directly beneath the summit. If you are roping up and swinging tools within minutes of leaving camp, you are on a serac or a crevasse wall low on the glacier, not on the headwall. The headwall is only reached after the whole gentle bowl has been crossed and the ground ahead of you rears up as one continuous face rather than a series of rolls.

A cross-check at the top of the ice: the summit should be directly above the headwall, not off to one side. If the wall in front of you tops out on a shoulder with more mountain visible beyond it, you have drifted around the bowl.

approach_variants.name: Water taxi up Ross Lake to the eastern shore, cutting out most of the trail
approach_variants.notes: The resort at the south end of Ross Lake runs a water taxi that will drop parties on the eastern shore, which removes most of the flat trail miles and turns the approach into the off-trail climb alone. It has to be booked ahead and the schedule and drop points change, so confirm directly before building a trip around it. The trade is that you are committed to a pickup time on a lake with no road out, so build slack into the plan rather than into the summit day.
approach_variants.season: Same window as the trail approach, but only once the boat service is running for the year
hazards: fixed pickup times on a lake with no road out
the same steep brushy cliff-banded timber belt above the shore
arriving late enough that the timber belt is done in the dark
crevasses on the glacier above
no reliable communication once off the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the landing the first task is to get onto the trail and find may creek - the East Bank Trail runs along this shore and the departure point is the creek, not a bearing. Once you leave the trail at May Creek every marker is identical to the walk-in variant: cliff bands from around 3,200 ft passed on game trails, continuous snow near 4,800 to 5,000 ft, and the flat bench just over 5,200 ft below the toe of the ice.

The one thing the boat changes is your margin, not your route. Parties dropped late in the day have started the timber belt in fading light, which is where the cliff bands become genuinely dangerous, because the passages through them are found by eye. If you cannot reach open ground above the bands in daylight, camp low rather than commit to the belt.

The negative marker is the same: if the ground ahead of you steepens into rock rather than easing onto snow, you are in a cliff band and should traverse to find the boot track rather than force it.

approach_variants.name: Before the highway opens: the gate at milepost 134
approach_variants.notes: The highway closes each winter between the gate west of the trailhead and a second gate far to the east, and reopens somewhere between mid-April and early summer depending on the year's damage and snowpack. Parties wanting the headwall in condition have started at the closed gate and covered the road on bikes or skis to the trailhead before starting the walk in. Everything above that is unchanged, except that the snow line is far lower and the timber belt may go faster on skis than it does on foot in summer.
approach_variants.season: Late winter and early spring, before the highway is cleared, when the headwall holds its best snow
hazards: avalanche terrain through the timber belt and on the glacier approach in early season
a long road section on bike or ski before the trip proper starts
short daylight and cold, with a committing position
cornices on the upper mountain
the road gate opening date moves year to year and can strand a plan
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The road section is navigation-free; the approach still starts at may creek. Ride or ski the closed highway to the trailhead near milepost 138 and pick up the East Bank Trail there. The departure from the trail is the creek, as in summer.

What changes is where the snow starts. In this window continuous snow is likely to begin well below the 4,800 to 5,000 ft line that summer parties describe, which means the cliff bands between roughly 3,200 ft and there are being crossed on snow rather than on game trails. A band that would be walked around in August may be a loaded slope in April. If the passage you would normally take through a band is a smooth, wind-loaded ramp rather than a boot track, treat it as avalanche terrain and not as a route.

The flat bench just over 5,200 ft below the glacier toe may be buried and unrecognisable as a bench; in that case the arrival marker is the change of angle where the ground stops climbing and the ice begins running away ahead of you toward the wall.

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and the Ptarmigan crest
approach_variants.notes: The prettier of the two ways in, and the one that puts you on the route's own ridge from the bottom. Mowich Lake sits at about 4,929 ft at the end of a road that has had no public access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed in April 2025 (before that it was often snowed shut into early or mid July), and that single fact decides whether this approach is available at all. From the lake it is three to four miles of trail up through Spray Park; at about 6,400 ft a beaten path breaks off right toward the permanent snow. Cross the Flett Glacier in the gap between Echo Rock, 7,870 ft, and Observation Rock, 8,364 ft, at somewhere around 7,500 ft, climb to the saddle immediately east of Observation Rock, and cross onto the Russell Glacier near 7,800 ft. From there the crest runs south, sometimes on rock but mostly on easy snow just left of the crest line, with the Russell falling away east. This stretch is uncrevassed and is genuinely a walk. The last few hundred yards to camp are not: the crest narrows to a knife edge with an overhanging rock step on it, and most parties bypass that by dropping about 200 ft onto 40 degree snow on the east side and traversing back. Well above the base, the exit gully through the rock buttress is the one identification climbers argue about — whether it is the first or the second break in the cliffs is genuinely unsettled, so climb to the fixed pin rather than to a count. The descent is the Emmons route out to White River, so coming in this way needs a car shuttle or a very long road walk.
approach_variants.season: June to early July
hazards: Ice avalanche off the Liberty Cap Glacier's ice cliffs onto the traverse between camp and the bergschrund
Bare rock at the crux chimney in lean years, which raises both the grade and the rockfall
Bergschrund and crevasses at the start of the technical ground, around 9,800 ft
Sustained 45 to 60 degree snow and ice, with a long exposed rising traverse
Rockfall off decomposing volcanic cliffs on everything below about 12,200 ft
Overhanging rock step on the knife edge into high camp
No road access to Mowich Lake since the April 2025 bridge closure, and a descent that finishes at a different trailhead
approach_variants.baseFinding: The walking and the climbing are cleanly separated here and the boundary is a flat spot, but the climb does not start above camp — it starts several hundred feet below it and on the far side of the ridge, and that is what parties get wrong. Follow the crest south from the saddle beside Observation Rock until the ridge stops rising and levels out at about 10,200 to 10,300 ft. You will know the place without being told, because four things sit together there and nowhere else: room for a couple of small tents on flat ground, a steep 2,000 ft drop to the Carbon Glacier immediately east of you, huge banded ice cliffs standing directly south above you where the Liberty Cap Glacier ends, and a clean view straight across at Liberty Ridge. From that camp the route drops west off the crest a few hundred feet onto the upper Mowich Glacier and crosses the bergschrund at about 9,800 ft, aiming for a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the middle of the face. Look that crossing over from camp the evening before, because it is in plain sight from up there and its condition changes year to year. The traverse down to it passes under the run-out of the ice cliffs and is usually walked across old avalanche debris and stray boulders sitting on the ice, so it is done in the dark and fast. Two ways to know you are wrong. If you have descended onto the Mowich Glacier and kept going west or south, you are wandering out onto Mowich Face ground rather than to the schrund. And if you cross a bergschrund with no ice cliffs above and to your left, stop: from the schrund the route rises back east, climber's left, toward those cliffs, not away from them. The route finishes on Liberty Cap; Columbia Crest is a separate trip across the summit plateau and is not part of this climb.

approach_variants.name: White River, St. Elmo Pass and across the Carbon
approach_variants.notes: The way in that is actually available during the ice season, because the White River road opens in late spring while Mowich Lake has had no road access since the 2025 bridge closure, and it puts you back at your own car after the Emmons descent instead of on the far side of the mountain. It is the Liberty Ridge approach as far as the Carbon: Glacier Basin, then a boot track up snow and scree to St. Elmo Pass, given variously as 7,400 or 7,600 ft, then onto the Winthrop Glacier and a roped traverse at roughly 7,200 to 7,400 ft around to Curtis Ridge, where there are good bivy sites near 7,500 ft. Next morning drop and cross the Carbon around 7,000 ft, staying clear of its seracs and north of the ice cliffs where the Russell calves onto it, then take snowfields up onto the Ptarmigan crest at about its 9,000 ft point and follow the ridge to high camp.
