It is longer than the Mowich walk, it crosses three glaciers, and it spends hours under actively shedding walls, so it wants to be done cold and early. One thing to fix in your head before the descent: parties coming off Liberty Cap routes routinely wander onto the busy Disappointment Cleaver at Columbia Crest instead of the faint Emmons track, which is the wrong side of the mountain if your car is at White River.
approach_variants.season: Mid-May to early July
hazards: Hours of exposure to rockfall and icefall crossing beneath Willis Wall and the Liberty Wall
Ice avalanche off the Liberty Cap Glacier's cliffs onto the traverse into the route
Crevasses on the Winthrop and the Carbon, thin bridges early and open cracks late
Committing traverse with no quick exit once past Curtis Ridge
Sustained 45 to 60 degree ice and a rock or mixed crux around 12,000 ft
Very little traffic, so no established track above the Carbon and a slow rescue
Losing the faint Emmons descent to the well-trodden Disappointment Cleaver at the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding: This is the approach on which Rainier's two Liberty Cap routes actually get confused, and the trap is a physical one: there is usually a bootpack running from St. Elmo Pass to the Carbon Glacier, and it was stamped in by parties going to Liberty Ridge. It is the right track as far as the Carbon and the wrong one after that. Working west you cross under Willis Wall and meet a narrow rock and snow ridge dropping straight to the glacier. That first spine is Liberty Ridge. Keep going. Past it the ground opens beneath a big pale cirque wall capped by hanging ice, and the next crest beyond that wall, roughly a mile and a half further west, is Ptarmigan Ridge. Put it the simple way and it is hard to get wrong: on Liberty Ridge the Liberty Wall is on your right, and on Ptarmigan Ridge it is on your left. Cross the Carbon below the seracs, gain the Ptarmigan crest at about its 9,000 ft point and follow the ridge up to the flat high camp at 10,200 to 10,300 ft. That flat is the base of the climb, and four things fix it together: room for a couple of small tents, a steep 2,000 ft drop to the Carbon immediately east, banded ice cliffs standing directly south above you where the Liberty Cap Glacier ends, and Liberty Ridge in full view straight across. From camp the route drops west off the crest onto the upper Mowich Glacier and crosses the bergschrund at about 9,800 ft, near a rock outcropping about the middle of the face — study that crossing from camp the evening before, because it is in plain sight from up there. Above the schrund the line rises back east, climber's left, toward the ice cliffs. If you have crossed a schrund with no ice cliff up and left of you, you are on the wrong part of the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Via the centre route's lower pitches
approach_variants.notes: You can scramble on up the gully to this climb's own ledge, but many parties add pitches instead: do the usual gully approach from the pullout near milepost 166 to the wall's upper ledge, then climb the lower pitches of the centre eleven-pitch line to the shared midway ledge system and traverse left from there. Rack for the pitches you are climbing to get there as well as for this route.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the wall has dried; the pitches used to reach it are the same ones that seep into early summer in wet years.
hazards: From the lower pitches, a retreat means reversing or rappelling somebody else's route
Loose and deteriorating rock on the lowest pitches and again high on the line
Belays are bolted but not all of them are rigged for rappel, so find the rappel stations before you need them
Everything below you is occupied ground; manage rockfall onto parties on the route you climbed in on
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are looking for a two-bolt anchor sitting on the midway ledge, and the trees are what place it: the anchor is on the ledge below a stand of trees, not level with them and not above them. Traverse left along the ledge until the trees are above you and the two bolts are at your feet. Confirm it from the rock: the first pitch off this anchor is a technical corner with loose chockstones at its hardest moves, so if what rises from your anchor is a clean face or a slab you are at the wrong station. Negative markers: if the anchor you have clipped is one of the bolted rappel stations belonging to the route you just climbed, you have not traversed at all; if the trees are still off to your left, you have not traversed far enough.

approach_variants.name: Via the right-hand cave route's lower pitches
approach_variants.notes: The same idea from the other side: climb the lower pitches of the right-hand cave line off the upper ledge to reach the shared midway ledge system, then traverse left. This is the longer leftward traverse of the two, so allow for it.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the wall has dried.
hazards: From the lower pitches, escape means rappelling a neighbouring line
Loose and deteriorating rock low and high on the route
Not all belays are rappel-rigged, so plan the descent before you leave the ledge
Long leftward traverse on a ledge with loose material on it
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the midway ledge, traverse left — further than from the centre line — until you find the two-bolt anchor set on the ledge directly below a stand of trees. The trees are the test: below them, not beside them. The first pitch above the anchor is a technical corner holding loose chockstones at the crux, which distinguishes it from the clean faces either side. Negative markers: if you are still passing bolted rappel stations that belong to the route you climbed up, keep traversing; if you have reached ground where the ledge system ends and the wall closes down, you have gone past it.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road walk, West Fork to Anderson Pass and the tarn camp
approach_variants.notes:
From US-101 at Brinnon, drive Dosewallips Road about 8.5 miles to the road-end parking and leave the car there; the road beyond has been closed to vehicles since the 2002 flood, and the washout itself is about a mile farther on. A mountain bike genuinely saves hours on the road miles. A short bypass trail with a few switchbacks gets round the washout, then the abandoned roadbed resumes for roughly 5.6 miles to the Dosewallips Ranger Station at about 1,600 ft.

From the ranger station take the Dosewallips River Trail 1.4 miles to the West Fork junction, then the West Fork Trail upstream past Dose Forks, Big Timber and Diamond Meadows to Honeymoon Meadows at 3,527 ft, roughly 8 trail miles on. Expect at least one calf-to-knee ford of the West Fork depending on snowmelt, and substantial blowdown — maintenance has lagged since the road closed. Beyond Honeymoon Meadows the trail climbs past Camp Siberia to Anderson Pass at 4,464 ft.

Leave the maintained trail at the pass and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to a camp on the snowy saddle above a small tarn at about 5,100 ft (Anderson or Valkyrie Lake). Most parties take 7-9 hours trailhead to camp. Fill up at the tarn; there is nothing above it.
approach_variants.season: Best spring to early summer, while the snow finger below Flypaper Pass is still continuous. By late summer that finger has thinned and steepened and the bergschrund above it has opened
hazards: Crevasses on the upper Eel Glacier, including large ones on its eastern slopes
A bergschrund at the head of the Eel that is hardest to cross late in the season, with a short steep step above it
The Flypaper Pass snow finger at 40-45 degrees, firm or icy, steeper than older descriptions state
Glide avalanches and cornice-triggered slides off the cliffs above the glacier terminus
Loose, crumbly meta-sedimentary rock on the final summit scramble
Unbridged fords and heavy blowdown on the West Fork trail, plus roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the climb is Flypaper Pass, and the test is which things are on which side of it. Flypaper Pass at about 6,500 ft is the notch between Mount Anderson on the east and Echo Rock (7,033 ft) on the west. Standing in the notch, Anderson is on your right and Echo Rock on your left when you are facing north through it. If both walls beside you are the same mountain, you are in a gully on a flank rather than in the pass.

The approach test, done before you can see the notch, is the tarn. From the camp saddle, traverse above the tarn — often still frozen — and take the single steep snow finger that runs up from the far side of it. There is one finger and it goes to one notch. If you are walking round the tarn at its level rather than above it, you have dropped too low and will meet cliffs.

Second test, and it is the one that says the pass is in the condition you planned for: the finger's steepest section now runs 40 degrees or more. Glacier recession has steepened it well beyond the older published figure of about 30 degrees over 300 vertical feet, so a party that finds it far steeper than the book has not gone the wrong way — those descriptions are old. If it has melted out to bare scree and ice, that is the season telling you to come back earlier, not a route-finding error.

What going too far looks like: over the pass the ground drops onto the Eel Glacier and a bergschrund cuts across below the headwall, forcing an end-around to one side. If you are on glacier and looking for a way past a schrund, you are past the base and onto the climb.

approach_variants.name: East Fork Quinault and Enchanted Valley to Anderson Pass from the west
approach_variants.notes:
Anderson Pass is a divide, and the Quinault side of it is a maintained trail too. From the Graves Creek trailhead at the end of the South Shore Quinault road, the East Fork Quinault Trail runs up the valley through Enchanted Valley to the pass. It is a longer valley walk than the Dosewallips side but it is a trail the whole way, with no closed road at the start and no West Fork fords, which in a wet year is the difference between the two.

At Anderson Pass the two approaches become one: leave the maintained trail and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to the tarn camp at about 5,100 ft, then the snow finger to Flypaper Pass.

Mileages published for the Quinault side vary widely with where the count starts and with the current state of the road, so none is quoted here.
approach_variants.season: Same window as the standard side — the pass and the snow finger above it decide the season, not the valley
hazards: Everything above the pass is the same: the 40-45 degree snow finger, the Eel Glacier crevasses and bergschrund, and loose summit rock
A long valley walk with river crossings and blowdown of its own
Arriving at the pass from the west means the shelter and the climbers' path are both below and behind you as you crest it
No cell coverage anywhere on either side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Identical to the Dosewallips variant above, because both arrive at Anderson Pass and everything above the pass is shared: traverse above the tarn, take the one steep snow finger from its far side, and know you are at Flypaper Pass when Mount Anderson is on one side of the notch and Echo Rock on the other.

The extra test this side needs is at the pass itself, because you arrive there from the opposite direction. Anderson Pass is a signed trail junction — the West Fork Dosewallips and East Fork Quinault trails meet there, with the Anderson Pass shelter (Camp Siberia) just below on the Dosewallips side at roughly 4,180 ft. The climbers' path leaves north off the pass and up the moraine. If you have walked over the pass and begun descending the other valley, you have missed the turn; it is a boot path, not a signed one.

approach_variants.name: Klahhane Ridge climbers' trail from Hurricane Ridge
approach_variants.notes: Paved path off the east end of the visitor centre lot, then open subalpine ridge for about two and a half miles to an unsigned split. A shorter, steeper start climbs from the Switchback Trail on the road below and joins higher up. Nothing dependable to drink past the visitor centre — carry it all.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Fractured, rotten rock on the summit block with holds that break
Rockfall funnelling down the crux gully onto anyone below
Rotten snow choking the summit notch into July and August
Exposed Class 3 moves with a fall of well over a hundred feet
Fast-building afternoon storms on a fully exposed ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbers' path leaves the maintained Klahhane Ridge Trail at an unsigned fork roughly 2.3 miles out: bear left and uphill to the west, where the maintained tread carries on right along the ridge toward Victor Pass and Lake Angeles. From the fork the primitive path climbs rocky meadow on the peak's west side and does about eight hundred of the day's feet in a little over half a mile, topping out near 6,000 ft in a scree bowl beneath the summit block. The identification that matters here is which notch, and it catches people every season: do not scramble the first notch you reach. The boot path keeps traversing higher and the gully that goes is further along, directly beneath the true summit. Stay on the worn tread climber's-left of the open scree fan rather than going straight up the fan itself, which is the rockfall funnel. You are at the base when the meadow ends and you are standing on dirty, fractured ledges with a roughly forty-foot exposed step above you. If the ground has levelled off or you are back on maintained tread heading toward Lake Angeles, you have overshot.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center (High Ridge Trail)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center lot

approach_variants.name: Mill Creek and the Azurite Pass side
approach_variants.notes: This is the approach the peak is normally catalogued under and the one that pairs naturally with Azurite. It runs from Highway 20 up Canyon Creek and then Mill Creek on tread that has seen little maintenance since the mine closed, where slide alder and downed timber are the recurring complaint and parties routinely lose the path entirely for stretches. A longer alternative from the West Fork Methow trailhead reaches the same country by way of the Pacific Crest Trail and Horse Heaven Camp and is often preferred for combined trips despite the extra mileage. Camp is usually made near the old mine or in the basin above it. Note that the point long marked on maps as Mount Ballard is a lower north sub-summit; the true high point lies about 1,100 ft further south and is slightly higher.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September
hazards: Slide alder and downed timber on an unmaintained approach trail
Route-finding through brush pockets and broken gullies on the flank
Loose, rotten rock and exposure near the summit ridge
Snowfields into July that can require an ice axe
Open upper mountain with full lightning exposure
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
approach_variants.baseFinding: On this side the walking ends at the old Azurite Mine site around 5,900 ft and the brush begins immediately. The base of the climb is the open basin at roughly 6,600 ft above and east of the mine, sitting between Ballard and the ridge running out toward Azurite. You know you are in it when the timber gives out and you can see the peak's flank in one piece above you rather than through trees. That flank is the difficulty: it is not a single clean face but a patchwork of brush pockets, rock ribs and short gullies, and parties consistently find that the hard part of the day is not the scrambling but picking which gully continues, a decision that comes to a head around 7,400 ft. Read the ground rather than committing early, because a gully that closes out costs a long reversal. The obvious-looking answer is a trap: the south ridge presents as a clean continuous line from below and is blocked higher by a notch with a gendarme in it, so a party that racks up the ridge crest on sight will be turned around. The other check is on which summit you are heading for. There are two high points on this mountain, and the northern one, the one carrying the old survey mark, is the lower; keep working south along the crest until the ground stops rising. If you find yourself on the connecting ridge with Azurite you have gone north and are on the wrong end of the massif.

approach_variants.name: South Fork Slate Creek and the east ridge
approach_variants.notes: The other side of the mountain, approached from the Slate Creek road system rather than from Mill Creek, and the line most parties who climb this peak actually use. It is shorter, the forest below camp is comparatively brush-free, and the route-finding above camp is far more legible than on the Mill Creek side, at the cost of one genuinely steep step low down and some exposed ledge work near the top. Snow conditions change this route's character completely: a filled-in slot low down and firm snow in the upper cirque make for fast travel, while dry late-season conditions leave loose rock and slippery vegetation. Camp is normally made in a scree basin below the east ridge.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: A steep vegetated step through the lowest cliff band, the hardest ground on the route
Exposed ledge traverse above the high saddle
Loose rock in the summit gully with a party stacked below
Steep snow in the east cirque into midsummer
Full lightning exposure on the open upper mountain
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
approach_variants.baseFinding: The approach has one unmistakable marker and the climb has another. Start at the locked gate on the Slate Creek road at about 3,800 ft and walk the South Fork road for roughly a mile and a half to an old vehicle bridge at about 4,000 ft; that bridge is the single positive check on the whole road walk, and if you have not crossed it you are still on the main branch. From the bridge, head south through open, brush-free forest for another mile and a half or so to a scree basin around 4,800 ft, the usual camp. From camp the route climbs through tight forest and then open scree to a shoulder on the east ridge at roughly 6,200 ft. The base of the real climbing is right there and it is easy to identify because it is the wrong colour: a steep slot of heather and grass cutting through the lowest cliff band, green vegetation in an otherwise rocky wall, and the only weakness in that band. It is the steepest ground on the route and it is the crux. Bare rock gullies to either side look more like a climb and are harder and looser, so the vegetated slot is the line. Above it stay on the rib and follow the ridge crest, then the scree slope and east cirque, to a high saddle north of the summit. From that saddle do not go straight up; traverse ledges, some of them exposed, to a narrow gully that gains the summit block.

approach_variants.name: Upper Trailhead on NFR 24, Trail #812 summer route
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, at the end of FS Road 2419-014 off FS 24 / FS 2419 — vault toilet, picnic table, Northwest Forest Pass required — Trail #812 climbs immediately. The first 0.3 mile is stacked stairstep switchbacks through forest, merging with the longer lower-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft.

From the merge, continue up the south ridge through increasingly open forest to timberline at about 4,500 ft, roughly a mile in. In summer conditions the trail is snow-free and well cut essentially to the top, switchbacking across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly subalpine meadows, threading a narrow notch and crossing west-facing slopes to the 5,944 ft summit. Total gain from the Upper Trailhead is 2,444 ft over 1.6 miles one way. No water on the upper route; carry all you need.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct for the snow-free summer trail; outside that the chute fills and the upper switchbacks are buried
hazards: The southeast-facing chute is an avalanche funnel that becomes sun-soaked and prone to wet slides by early-mid afternoon — start early and check NWAC in spring
Chute-bordering rocks are extremely slick when wet or in fog
Losing the trail under snow leads onto steeper, looser ground
A very popular and crowded trail with kicked-loose rock from parties above
No water on route
Fragile subalpine vegetation on the open upper slopes
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The decision point on this mountain is a signed junction at timberline, roughly 4,500 ft, and a sign is the best fog marker there is because it does not depend on visibility beyond arm's length. At that junction the winter climbing route breaks right, straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute, and the maintained summer trail switchbacks left across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly meadows. This variant is the left one.

If you find yourself climbing a single steep funnel-shaped gully rather than working a series of switchbacks, you have taken the right-hand branch and you are on the winter route.

Second test, higher: the summer trail threads a narrow notch and then crosses west-facing slopes before the final approach to the summit. Many of its switchbacks have stairstep risers built into them. Built steps are man-made and unambiguous underfoot. If you are on trackless scree you have left the trail.

Honest limit, and it is seasonal rather than navigational: outside roughly November to June, snow fills the chute and buries the upper switchbacks, and most parties then climb the chute directly because the summer trail is not there to be found. That is not a route-finding failure; it is a different route, and it demands an ice axe and traction. The rocks in and bordering the chute are notoriously slick when wet even outside full winter conditions — that is an official Forest Service warning, not a trip-report opinion.

approach_variants.name: Lower Trailhead, the long approach to the same trail
approach_variants.notes:
The Lower Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft, 3.1 miles one way, and takes no fee. It welcomes you with an easy grade rather than the upper trailhead's near-immediate jolt, and it is the sensible choice when FS Road 2419-014 to the upper lot is snowed in or gated.

It climbs steadily through forest and joins the upper-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft. Everything above the merge is identical.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Oct, and it is snow-free earlier than the upper road in some years
hazards: Same as the upper-trailhead variant, over a longer and gentler approach
The 3,900 ft merge is where parties descend to the wrong trailhead
No water on the upper route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The first test is the merge at about 3,900 ft, where the lower trail joins the upper-trailhead trail. From below, that junction is the confirmation you are on the right path at all; from above it is the fork you take downhill to get back to the lower lot rather than the upper one. Parties have descended to the wrong car here.

The decision point is the same signed junction at timberline, roughly 4,500 ft, about 2.5 miles from the lower trailhead: the winter climbing route breaks right up the chute, the summer trail switchbacks left. Take the left.

And the same confirmations above it: stairstep risers built into the switchbacks, a narrow notch, and west-facing slopes before the summit.

approach_variants.name: The winter chute, direct from the timberline junction
approach_variants.notes:
Not a different trailhead but a genuinely different climb, and it is what most parties are on outside core summer because the summer switchbacks are buried. From either trailhead, follow Trail #812 to the signed timberline junction at about 4,500 ft and take the right-hand branch straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute below the summit saddle.

This demands an ice axe and traction — crampons or microspikes — and it is steep, funnel-shaped slide-path terrain with real avalanche potential. Check avalanche conditions before going up.

It is also the fast descent when conditions allow: with an axe carried in self-arrest position, parties glissade roughly 1,000 ft in a couple of minutes. That is consequential terrain rather than a casual slide.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Nov-Jun, while the chute holds a firm continuous snowpack
hazards: A steep funnel-shaped slide path with real avalanche potential; check NWAC before going
Wet-slide danger by early-mid afternoon in spring on a sun-soaked southeast aspect
Exposed rocks and ice bulges lower in the chute as snow thins — glissading then becomes dangerous
An uncontrolled glissade or a fall on hard snow without self-arrest skill on genuinely consequential terrain
Slick chute-bordering rocks when wet or in fog
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the signed timberline junction at about 4,500 ft and the right-hand branch out of it. That is the whole test and it is the same sign the summer parties turn left at. The chute is the prominent scree-and-snow funnel that runs straight up toward the summit saddle from there — there is one, it is obvious, and it is the reason the junction is signed at all.

The confirming test is that the ground stops switchbacking. The summer trail traverses; the chute goes up the fall line. If you are still zig-zagging you took the left branch.

The test for whether you should be there at all, which matters more on this route than finding it: the chute is south-east facing and sun-soaked, and by early-to-mid afternoon in spring it is prone to wet slides. Start early. Later in the season, as the snow thins and exposes talus, rock and ice bulges, the chute stops being the fast line and becomes the dangerous one — at that point the correct call is the summer switchbacks for the whole descent.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Upper Trailhead (elev. ~3,500 ft, at the end of FS Road 2419-014 off FS 24/FS 2419 - the lot has a vault toilet, picnic table, and requires a Northwest Forest Pass), Trail #812 climbs immediately.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin, over the col and across the Gloomy Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Same walk in as for Seven Fingered Jack and Maude: Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing at about 4,140 ft, then the steep unmaintained climbers' trail on the north side of the creek into Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft.

This is the common approach but not the elegant one. It exists because the alternative is the ferry up Lake Chelan to Holden and the Railroad Creek trail into Copper Basin, which gains the East Ridge — the standard route — much more directly. A third option starts at Cottonwood on the Entiat River and reaches the East Ridge by way of the Entiat Glacier. All three converge on the same south-east face finish.

From Leroy Basin, head north-west toward a waterfall and climb its left side to a small notch on the ridge of Seven Fingered Jack. Published descriptions of this saddle vary — one places it just west of an obvious 7,700 ft col with a couple of bivy sites at the low point, another gives it as a notch reached past a second creek crossing — and they may or may not be the same feature, so check it on a map rather than assuming.

From the saddle you must drop about a thousand feet into the moraine at the terminus of the Gloomy Glacier, and every foot of it has to be regained on the way out. Two published ways down: descend to the tarn below and go around a prominent rock formation that guards the basin, or descend to the right across sandy ledges and down large boulders.

Expect roughly nine hours round trip from Leroy Basin, and a very long day car to car — one party left the trailhead at three in the morning and got back at eleven at night.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing runs through avalanche terrain earlier than that
hazards: A thousand feet of descent into the Gloomy basin that must be regained on the way out
Avalanche terrain on the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing
Icy forty-degree slopes near the top of the Gloomy Glacier, with crevasses below the usual line
Two thousand feet of exceptionally loose talus and scree above the basin
The narrow exposed ledge traverse off the col, which is avoidable and should be avoided
Route-finding is the crux — this is regarded as the most complex of the three Entiat nine-thousanders
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Fernow is not visible from Leroy basin, and this is confirmed rather than folklore. Parties climbing the basin under the cirque of Seven Fingered Jack report having real difficulty identifying the route because the peak simply is not in view. Do not stand in the basin trying to pick your line off the mountain; you cannot see it. Carry a track.

The arrival test is short and physical: cross the moraine below the Gloomy Glacier, go up the waterfall, and you are in the broad basin below Fernow. That is where the climbing starts.

Above that basin there are two decision points and both have a wrong answer that is on record.

First: descend the glacier to its terminal moraine at about 6,500 ft, then climb the right side of a stream to an upper snow-filled basin, and from there go south-west up a broad gully that turns eastward. That is Class 2-3 and gives you the luxury of knowing where you are. The alternative — dropping only to 7,000 ft and making a rising traverse through a succession of gullies, ribs and small cliffs — is Class 3-plus with snow and ice and the feeling of being lost somewhere in the Entiat Mountains.

Second, and this is the one that matters: from the broad gully, do not go all the way to the col and traverse the south-east face on the narrow ledges there. They are described as exposed enough to frighten a bird, with the honest observation that a fallen body would be unlikely to be found. Instead climb the broad gully to about 8,400 ft, then a loose gully to about 9,000 ft, and traverse the face at nine thousand on a wide ledge that is not exposed at all.

The 8,400 ft mark is a real landmark rather than a number on a map — two independent parties record the ground changing character there, one of them at a large bench holding permanent snow with water running off it. From 8,400 the line goes up loose talus to the ridge between Seven Fingered Jack and Fernow, where cairns pick up and weave around to the south-east ridge of the summit block. The cairns are reported by three separate parties, though one notes they stop near the summit itself.

The general principle behind all of it: climb as far as you can up the ridge separating Fernow's south-east and south-west faces. Once on the East Ridge, a couple of hundred feet of Class 3 on reasonably solid rock finishes it.

approach_variants.name: Climb East Fury first; the traverse starts on its summit
approach_variants.notes:
This route has no approach of its own in the ordinary sense. It is the connecting ridge between the two summits of Mount Fury, and the only way to arrive at its start is to have climbed East Fury, which is reached from the Ross Dam Trailhead by water taxi to Big Beaver Landing, the Big Beaver Creek Trail, the Access Creek bushwhack, Access Col, Luna Col and the Southeast Glacier.

Budget the East Fury ascent as a full day in its own right before this one begins, and note that the traverse is about half a kilometre of ridge, which says nothing useful about how long it takes.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Poor-quality anchors on chossy rock, with each rappel making retreat harder
A committing position on a ridge between two of the most remote summits in the range
Loose class 2-3 talus on the descent of East Fury's east side
The whole outing sits behind a full day's climb of East Fury and a multi-day approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of this route is a summit, which is the one thing on a mountain you cannot walk past. You are at the start when you are standing on the top of East Fury with the ridge running west toward the West Peak. There is no gully to find, no bench to identify and no chance of starting the wrong line: if you are not on East Fury's summit, you have not started.

What that means in practice, and it is a decision rather than a landmark: the commitment happens at the first rappel, not at the summit. Getting off each tower on the traverse means rappelling off poor-quality anchors on chossy rock, and each rappel down makes retreat progressively harder. The place to decide whether the weather and the hour justify the traverse is on East Fury's summit, before the first pull.

What going too far looks like, on the other end: once off the traverse, the way home is back over East Fury and down its east side to the saddle on loose class 2-3 talus, then down the Southeast Glacier to Luna Col. Descending anywhere off the north side of the connecting ridge drops you into Luna Cirque, 2,400 ft below the col you camped at.

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass, the crest trail to Methow Pass, and the east ridge
approach_variants.notes: The long way, and the one that suits a two-day trip. From the large paved lot on the north side of SR-20 at Rainy Pass, follow the crest trail north as it climbs steadily through subalpine forest and larch parkland past Porcupine Creek — fill up there, it is the last easy water before a long dry stretch of switchbacks — to Cutthroat Pass. From the pass the trail drops toward Granite Pass and a saddle beyond it, where a steep snowfield often lasts into August and has caused slide-for-life falls, so carry an axe if you are early in the season. Beyond, the trail contours across open, sparsely treed slopes to Snowy Creek Meadow, a common water and camp stop, with a short side trail west into the Snowy Lakes basin for a higher and more scenic bivy under Tower Mountain and Golden Horn. From the meadow, stay on the crest trail north to the open plateau at Methow Pass and leave it there: travel west and southwest off-trail through open heather and talus benches toward the peak's east ridge, gain the ridge, and follow moderate sand, scree and talus — loose in places, with real route-finding — up to the saddle between the true summit and its lower false summit.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September, with July through September giving the driest scree. June ascents work but the final slopes and gully still hold snow and want an axe and crampons. The highway is shut for avalanche control through the winter, which closes both approaches outright.
hazards: loose scree, talus and blocky rock on the unmarked upper route, worst near the summit saddle and the final gully
a steep lingering snowfield just past Granite Pass that has caused slide-for-life falls into August
a long, mostly off-trail final leg with no marked line
afternoon thunderstorms and fast weather changes on exposed ridge crest and passes
wildfire smoke reducing visibility in late summer
seasonal closure of the highway cutting off road access entirely
approach_variants.baseFinding: The saddle you are aiming for sits between the true summit and a lower knob to its east — do not stop on the knob. From Methow Pass, get up onto the east ridge as early as you can and keep close to its crest; the talus slopes below it are loose and slow, and parties who angle across them lose time. Moderate sand, scree and talus lead to the saddle between the summit and the eastern false summit. From the saddle, several hundred feet of blocky Class 2-3 scrambling on rock that takes hands reach the top. If the highest ground you can reach still has something higher a short distance to the west, you are on the knob, and the saddle below it is where you cross to the true summit.

approach_variants.name: Swamp Creek pullout and the south ridge
approach_variants.notes: The short, steep alternative, and the way most day parties go. Start from the highway pullout at Swamp Creek and climb through brushy forest to the foot of the prominent ridge on the mountain's south side. Follow the ridge upward, staying on the crest where it lets you and moving climber's right to get around the cliff bands that block the crest around 5,200 ft — getting that traverse wrong is what turns parties back. Above the cliff bands the ridge opens out onto sand and scree and continues to the summit block. This side faces the sun and dries early, which is why it comes into condition before the crest-trail approach and why it turns into a loose, dusty grind by late summer; a snow finger on this flank can hold firm snow at a fairly steep angle into early summer, which speeds the ascent considerably for a party carrying an axe.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September once the snow finger has stabilised or melted, with July and August driest. Earlier in the season the finger is a snow climb rather than a scramble.
hazards: cliff bands around 5,200 ft where the crest is blocked and the bypass is on climber's right — the main route-finding failure on this side
a steep snow finger on this flank into early summer, with wet-slide and sluff potential
brushy forest on the lower ridge with no maintained tread
loose scree and blocky rock on the upper route and in the final gully
an exposed ridge crest with no shelter from afternoon thunderstorms
seasonal closure of the highway cutting off road access entirely
approach_variants.baseFinding: The notch is on the far side of the block from where you arrive, and you have to traverse to it. At about 7,200 ft the ridge you have been following runs into the summit block; leave the crest there and scramble loose scree and granite blocks across the east side — climber's right — until you reach a notch tucked under the summit block. Cross the notch, and the way on is a short, shallow gully leading up to the top. That gully is the marker: it is shallow and blocky rather than deep and cut, and it is the only break that goes at scrambling grade. If the block above you is unbroken wall, keep traversing right rather than starting up; if you have dropped far enough to be under steep cliff bands, you have gone too low and should regain height. The upper ground is several hundred feet of enjoyable blocky scrambling on rock that takes hands, and a lower false summit sits beside the true one — if the highest ground you can reach still has something higher a short distance away, you are on the false summit and the saddle between them is where you crossed.

approach_variants.name: Merritt Lake Trailhead and Nason Ridge Trail to Crescent Lake
approach_variants.notes: The shorter and more direct way in. From the highway turn onto the rough forest road — high clearance is worth having — and drive to the Merritt Lake Trailhead. Climb the Merritt Lake trail to the lake, then join the Nason Ridge Trail and follow it east to Crescent Lake, which sits below the peak's south side. Water is available at Crescent Lake but is unreliable higher on the mountain, so fill there. The trail is well defined the whole way to the lake, and everything above it is your own route-finding.
approach_variants.season: July into October once the ridge clears; snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring.
hazards: Several little bowls look like the peak's south face and one of them is the wrong drainage entirely
A well-worn boot path leaves the ridge trail heading north — that is the climbers' route to the neighbouring summit, not this one
No established route above Crescent Lake, and the descent is the crux of the day
Loose, dirty Class 3 in whichever gully you pick through the cliff band
Slippery grass and dense alder low on the face when descending
Water unreliable above Crescent Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: Make sure you are in the right drainage before you climb — several little bowls look like this face, and the one to your east is Royal Creek. That is the single mistake worth guarding against here, and it is made before you gain any height. From the northeast side of Crescent Lake, take the talus field at the head of the lake, directly below the obvious cliff band; a short thrash through woody brush leads to an upper talus field, and from there drift right to get around the cliff. Several gullies break the band and there is no single correct one — parties pick the easiest-looking line and find it loose, dirty Class 3 for about a hundred feet. That crux band is the confirmation you are on the face, not a sign to retreat, but it is unpleasant to reverse, so note your line. Above it the ground eases onto talus and dirt climbers' paths to the top. Note also that a well-worn boot path leaves the ridge trail heading north on the way in: that is the climbers' route to the neighbouring peak and not the way to this one.

approach_variants.name: Rock Mountain Trailhead via Rock Lake and the Rock–Crescent col
approach_variants.notes: The longer and more scenic way in, and the one commonly used by parties who want the neighbouring summit in the same outing. From the highway near the milepost, climb the Rock Mountain trail to Rock Lake — snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring on this side — then cross the col between the two peaks near 6,500 ft and descend roughly nine hundred feet on the far side to Crescent Lake. From there the climb is the same as from the other trailhead. It costs a substantial descent that has to be regained on the return, which is the price of the extra ground it covers.
approach_variants.season: July into October. Snow lingers above about 5,000 ft into late spring and the col holds it longest.
hazards: A substantial descent to Crescent Lake that must be reclimbed on the way out
Snow persisting on the col into late spring
Several little bowls look like the peak's south face — confirm the drainage before climbing
The same cliff band and loose, dirty Class 3 gullies above the lake
A long day made longer by the added distance and the col crossing
approach_variants.baseFinding: Crescent Lake is the common starting point, and on this side you arrive at it from above. Cross the col between the two peaks and descend several hundred feet on the far side to the lake; the tell that you are on this variant rather than the direct one is that you reach the water losing height rather than gaining it. From the lake the climb is identical, and so is the mistake to guard against: several little bowls in this basin look like the peak's south face, and being sure of the drainage before you start upward matters more than anything higher on the route. Take the talus field at the head of the lake directly below the obvious cliff band, push through the woody brush to an upper talus field, then drift right to get round the cliff. Several gullies break the band, none of them the single correct one; expect about a hundred feet of loose, dirty Class 3 in whichever you choose. Above it, talus and dirt climbers' paths lead to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Park Creek Pass and the heather traverse to the Fremont saddle and the hogsback
approach_variants.notes:
The standard start is the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 130, about 1,060-1,200 ft, and the Thunder Creek trail north for roughly 16-18 miles to the Thunder Basin camp area around 6,000 ft and on to Park Creek Pass. A southern alternative reaches the same pass from Stehekin: the High Bridge guard station near 1,600 ft, the Stehekin River trail to the Park Creek trailhead, then the Park Creek trail past Buckner Camp — with a creek crossing on a less-than-substantial footlog that is genuinely nerve-wracking in the dark.

From Park Creek Pass leave the maintained trail and traverse gradually northward around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, roughly a mile and a half to two miles, crossing a rib around 7,600 ft and a steep gully through cliff bands around 7,350 ft that can hold snow or ice. That brings you to the Fremont Glacier saddle around 8,000-8,250 ft, where rock-outcrop bivy sites with nearby running water make the standard high camp.

From camp it is about three and a half hours to the summit.
approach_variants.season: July and August
hazards: Crevasses on the Fremont Glacier, generally small but present — rope up
A bergschrund that opens below the summit ridge as the snow finger melts out late season, and a moat where the glacier meets the crest
Exposed, often unroped class 3-4 scrambling on the summit ridge
Long unmaintained cross-country route-finding above the moraine camp
Footlog crossings over Thunder and Park creeks that are hazardous at night or in high water
No fixed anchors anywhere on the route — a rappel off the summit block has to be built from a horn, a chockstone or a picket
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the Hogsback — the snow spine at the upper edge of the Fremont Glacier, on the peak's south ridge. You reach it by a gentle glacier crossing from the saddle camp, and there is a moat crossing to step from the snow onto the crest, which late in the season may have no bridge left at all. Snow spine plus a gap to step across is the confirmation you are at the start.

Then count three features in order, and the order is the whole route-finding problem: a class 3-4 rock pitch gains a left-slanting ramp — a fault-line weakness in the cliff bands — to the summit ridge; then exposed class 2-3 ledges on the east side of the ridge lead through a U-notch between the summit tower and the south horn; then a final class 3-4 pitch of about 100 ft on good holds and solid rock reaches the tiny summit.

The strongest negative test is the ramp: if you are trying to climb the summit tower directly from the glacier, you have missed it. The ramp is the way through the cliff bands and it slants left. Going straight at the tower puts you on ground the route deliberately avoids.

The U-notch is the second confirmation and it is a shape, not a height: a U-shaped gap between the summit tower and the south horn, reached by traversing ledges on the ridge's east flank. If you never dropped onto the east side, you did not take the ledges.

And know which side of the mountain you are on before you start: this is the southeast/southwest approach, from Park Creek Pass. The Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder on the west; the Banded Glacier route comes from Fisher Creek and gains the northeast ridge at about 8,800 ft. All three finish on the same summit block and share nothing below it.

approach_variants.name: Fisher Creek to the lake camp, over the ridge onto the Banded Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Two ways in, and which one you use depends on whether SR-20 is open. The always-open option is the Thunder Creek trail from Colonial Creek Campground near 1,200 ft for about nine miles to the Fisher Creek trail junction, then the Fisher Creek trail about three miles — past a good log bridge with a handrail — to a lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier. Roughly thirteen miles one way. The shorter option is Easy Pass from SR-20 near milepost 151, over the pass at 6,500 ft and down into Fisher Basin, about ten miles, but the trailhead is gated by the highway's seasonal closure.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge — sometimes called Christmas Tree Col — which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.
approach_variants.season: June and July
hazards: A major crevasse crossed on a narrow snow bridge on the Banded Glacier
Talus lying on top of bullet-hard glacier ice, described as a pile of marbles — treacherous in a whiteout descent
Cliff bands above the lake camp
Loose chossy rock on the summit ridge and rockfall in the approach gullies
Heavy mosquitoes in the lake basin through June and July
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The critical transition is a negative test: gain the northeast ridge on solid rock at about 8,800 ft rather than attempting the summit block directly from the glacier. That is the base of the climbing and it is the single thing this route can get wrong. If you are trying to climb off the ice straight at the summit, you have skipped the transition — cross the glacier until you can step onto solid rock on the ridge, and only then start up.

Getting there is a sequence of two cols and they are different things. First, from the lake camp near 5,160 ft, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge — sometimes called Christmas Tree Col — and drop over it onto the Banded Glacier. Second, ascend the Banded to the Banded-Douglas Col, which is literally the saddle between the two named glaciers. A col you crossed to reach ice, and a col you reached by climbing ice, are not the same feature.

So the question that settles your position in fog is which glacier is under you: this route travels between two named glaciers, so if you can identify which one you are standing on, you know which stage you are at. The Banded is the one you drop onto from the ridge above camp; the Douglas is on the far side of the col above.

And all three Logan routes end on the same 300 ft of class 3-4 summit block, so the summit confirms nothing. What distinguishes them is entirely below: this one comes from Fisher Creek and a lake camp; the Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder; the Fremont Glacier route comes from Park Creek Pass on the other side of the mountain.

Watch the scree below the glacier on the way up with the descent in mind — it is unstable enough that parties note it climbs far better than it downclimbs.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col
approach_variants.notes: Drive the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, roughly twenty-four miles and turn right onto the Phelps Creek road, FR 6211, to the trailhead at about 3,500 ft. The trail up the valley is the same tread hikers use for Spider Meadow. Walk the Phelps Creek trail, #1511, about three and a half flat miles to where it meets Leroy Creek near 4,120 to 4,140 ft. Cross on a large tree or by rock-hopping — awkward in early season with the creek up — and pick up the well-worn but unsigned climbers' trail, #1512, on the north side of the creek. It is sometimes called the Carne Mountain High Route, but the two are also treated as different paths, so do not assume the names are interchangeable. It climbs steeply, then eases into the Leroy Creek Basin meadow at about 6,100 ft, roughly five miles from the car and a little over two hours for a party moving well with light packs. Good camping and water. Above the basin, one party continued on the high-route path less than a quarter mile and then went directly into the upper basin below Maude by way of a gully with a small waterfall. Keep climbing cross-country over meadow, scrub, talus and probably snow to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col at about 8,150 ft, north-west of Maude's summit.
approach_variants.season: Best while the face still holds continuous snow and ice, roughly Jun into mid-Jul; it used to hold year round and no longer does
hazards: Cornice at the top of the face — parties have had pieces release across their tracks
Four hundred feet of exposed descending traverse from the col on snow, ice and very loose Class 3
Sixty-degree snow for the first moves off the traverse
Leroy Creek crossing running high in early season
Very poor rock quality throughout this group of peaks
Descending a west-side gully by mistake instead of continuing south toward Ice Lakes
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The col is not the route, and that is the thing to internalise before you get there. From the col you have to go down about four hundred feet, and not in one clean line — it comes in a series of forced descents alternating with traverses.

The recorded sequence: from the col, take the option toward the Entiat River valley side, downclimb roughly a hundred feet of face to a moderate bench, traverse a couple of hundred yards, be forced down again, traverse again, and eventually arrive at a steep snow slope beneath an overhang. That slope is the steepest ground of the day, around sixty degrees for the first moves, easing above.

The test is visual and it is unambiguous: you have descended far enough when the face comes into full view. Until it does, you are still traversing. One party took an hour and a half from the col to standing on continuous snow at the foot of the face.

Once on it, the lower face runs around thirty-five to forty degrees. A rib on the right side of the face is the line parties choose, not because it is named but because it keeps you out from under the cornice.

What not to expect: a bergschrund. The 1957 first ascent, coming from below on the Ice Lakes side, stood at a schrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above. Parties arriving by the col traverse enter partway up the face and bypass that ground entirely, and modern reports of this approach do not mention a schrund at all. The hazard people actually record here is the cornice at the top — one party had a piece of it come down and sweep across their tracks.

Honest gap worth knowing: nothing published tells you how to distinguish Maude's north face from Seven Fingered Jack's. The two, with Fernow, form one continuous headwall at the head of the Entiat, so the col is your positional anchor rather than the look of the wall.

On the way down, stay south and descend toward Ice Lakes. Parties regularly drop into one of the gullies cut into Maude's west side, either by mistake or thinking it a shortcut, and it is not.

approach_variants.name: Entiat River and Ice Lakes from the east — the first-ascent line
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Entiat River Road and walk the Entiat River trail #1400 about eight and a quarter miles to the Ice Creek trail. The Entiat River has to be crossed on logs, and if there is no log at the trail there may be a large jam south of it.

The first-ascent party did not follow the river to the meadows at its head. They walked instead to the col between Spectacle Buttes and Maude's south-east side and dropped from Ice Lakes onto the slopes beside the face, judging it more direct and free of bushwhacking. That cost them nearly three thousand feet of climbing to reach Ice Lakes.
approach_variants.season: Same window; this side is a much longer walk and is mostly used by parties already camped at Ice Lakes or exiting that way
hazards: Unbridged crossing of the Entiat River on logs
Bergschrund at the foot of the face on this side
A very long walk in on a trail that has burned in the past
Cornice at the top of the face
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base-finding here is one moment rather than a sequence: after the long grind up to Ice Lakes, you come over the crest and the face is right there in front of you. The first-ascent account says exactly that — the doubts about having picked the right way vanished on cresting the ridge.

Coming from this side you meet the face at its foot rather than partway up, which is the real difference from the col approach. That means descending steep snow slopes to a snowfield, then up to the glacier, and standing at the bergschrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above — around two thousand feet of it on the first ascent, averaging forty to forty-five degrees and over forty-five near the top.

So the test is which problem you are handed. If you are looking up at a schrund at the bottom of the whole face, you came from below. If you never saw one, you came across from the col.

approach_variants.name: Low Divide and Seattle Basin to the Noyes–Meany col
approach_variants.notes: Low Divide is reached up the North Fork Quinault, or from the Elwha with a long road walk or ride added at the start. Almost nobody comes for this peak alone — it is normally tagged while linking Christie, Meany and Seattle from one camp near the divide or in Seattle Basin.
approach_variants.season: Late July to mid-September
hazards: Steep snow fingers in the approach cols into early summer
Loose rock on the cliff bands below the summit cirque
Eroded, compacted sidehill gullies on the traverse beneath the peak
An Elwha ford at Chicago Camp that is hazardous at high water
Extreme remoteness — any rescue is a multi-day affair
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of this climb is a col rather than a face, and it is the same gateway parties heading for Meany use. From camp near Low Divide or in Seattle Basin, cross the head of Seattle Creek and work up talus and heather to the saddle between Noyes and Meany, gained by a loose rock couloir that tops out on a patch of snow. Standing in it, Meany's summit block is the abrupt tower on the north side and Noyes is the broader, lower ground opposite; the standard slopes leave the col directly and there is no gully mouth or rock step to identify, so the col itself is the landmark. The long sidehill traverse across eroded gullies that gets you there is the approach, not the climb, and the several similar-looking chutes cut into it do not go — resist the temptation to start up the first one that points at the summit. Above the col the ground is Class 2 to 3 along the summit ridge. If you find yourself over the far side and dropping toward the Elwha headwaters, you have crossed the divide instead of turning up it.

approach_variants.name: Paradise, the Nisqually crossing and the Wilson bench
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise (5,420 ft) follow the paved trail about a mile to Glacier Vista, then the Nisqually Moraine climbers' path to roughly 6,300 ft where boot paths drop onto the Nisqually Glacier. Rope up here — the crossing is through crevassed ground exposed to icefall from above and is dangerous in poor visibility.

From the east side of the glacier there are two ways onto the Wapowety Cleaver ground. One is a flat traverse to the base of a gully known as The Fan, climbed directly to a bench at about 7,300 ft; The Fan carries avalanche, rockfall and steep-snow hazard. The other climbs the Nisqually/Wilson margin at about 6,800 ft through an often-crevassed gully to the same 7,300–7,400 ft bench.

Above the bench, snow slopes lead to a string of established camps: Wilson Moraine (8,200–8,600 ft), Lower Castle (9,250 ft) and Upper Castle (9,400–9,500 ft), the most common base, with running water from about mid-June. Higher again, rock islands along the west edge of the Turtle snowfield between roughly 9,500 and 10,500 ft hold good bivouacs, and there is usually flowing water at the snowfield edges in warm weather.

Camp Hazard (about 10,800 ft) is the traditional high camp and is named for what sits above it: the Kautz Ice Cliff. Many parties deliberately camp lower and climb through Camp Hazard early rather than sleep under the cliff. On the Turtle, keep to the western, climber's-left side — the centre and east are raked by ice and rock off the cliff.

Rainier permits apply: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, and a wilderness permit for each overnight camp in the high-use season.
approach_variants.season: Mid-May into early August; the approach and glaciers deteriorate quickly after that
hazards: Serac fall from the Kautz Ice Cliff onto Camp Hazard and the traverse beneath it
Crevasses and icefall exposure on the Nisqually Glacier crossing
Avalanche, rockfall and steep snow in The Fan gully
Ice and rockfall raking the centre and east side of the Turtle snowfield
Thin or rotten ice in the chute late in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The single most useful fact about this route is that the technical climbing starts below Camp Hazard, not above it. Parties who expect to walk out of camp and start climbing walk straight under the ice cliff.

From camp, pick up the climbers' path on the rock and follow it to a short rappel, which often has a fixed line on it. That rappel is the confirmation you are on the right line — it drops you about 150 ft into the drainage gully at the bottom of the ice cliff. You should be losing height before you gain any.

From the bottom of that gully, traverse west, underneath the ice cliff, until you can see an obvious snow-and-ice ramp running up on your left. That ramp is the Kautz ice chute, and it is the start of the route. The older description of the same ground is: down over the ridge, down the gully about 150 ft, then either cross the icefall into the broad chute or continue down and around the toe of the icefall to reach the bottom of the chute.

What you should find in the chute: two steps of alpine ice separated by lower-angle snow. The first is the easier, anything from a short pitch of steep snow to about 250 ft of ice; the second is the crux, from a short pitch to more than 300 ft, steeper, and where a second tool earns its place. Both change a great deal from year to year. In lean years the ice can be thin, rotten or frozen dirt rather than good ice; the angle, not the quality, is what identifies it.

Negative marker: if you are climbing directly up from Camp Hazard toward the ice cliff, stop. That is the serac fall line, and it is the reason the camp has its name.

approach_variants.name: Comet Falls and Van Trump Park
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Comet Falls trailhead (3,650 ft) on the Longmire–Paradise road. The maintained Comet Falls Trail climbs 2.2 miles and about 2,000 ft to a junction, then continues toward Van Trump Park for another 0.6 miles to the end of maintained tread. From there unmaintained social trails climb a steep moraine crest to about 6,500 ft and onto the permanent snow of the Van Trump Glacier remnant, which is followed to the Upper Castle at roughly 9,500 ft where this approach merges with the Paradise line.

The advantage is that it never crosses the Nisqually Glacier. The cost is a lower start, a steeper carry and a descent that is genuinely hard to reverse: the Park Service's own advice is to save a GPS track, because relocating the correct moraine and the treeline trail junction on the way down is difficult even in clear weather. Several parties a season lose that junction and end up bushwhacking.
approach_variants.season: Same window; avoids the Nisqually Glacier crossing entirely
hazards: Losing the moraine crest and the treeline trail junction on descent — carry a saved track
Steep unmaintained moraine travel above the end of maintained trail
Same serac and ice-cliff exposure above the Castle and at Camp Hazard
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variant's finding problem is the reverse of most: the hard recognition is on the way down, not the way up. On the way up, the sequence is trail to a junction, more trail to the end of maintained tread, then a steep moraine crest — if you are still on graded tread above about 6,500 ft you have followed the wrong branch toward Van Trump Park's meadows rather than the climbers' line.

The merge point is the Upper Castle at about 9,400–9,500 ft, a rock rib with established camp sites and, from mid-June, running water. Once you are there the route ahead is the same as the Paradise approach: up the Turtle keeping to its western edge, to Camp Hazard, and then down a short rappel into the gully beneath the ice cliff to reach the chute.

approach_variants.name: Paradise and Glacier Vista, across the Nisqually to the Turtle and Camp Hazard
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise at 5,400 ft, the common approach follows the Skyline Trail to Glacier Vista and the Nisqually Moraine, then drops west onto the glacier. The route crosses the lower Nisqually, gains the Wilson Glacier and climbs to the Turtle Snowfield, with camps at The Castle around 9,200-9,500 ft and Camp Hazard at 10,800 ft at the top of the snowfield.

Roped travel and crevasse-rescue readiness are needed from the moment you leave the Nisqually. Water is available from snowmelt lower down on the Comet Falls and Van Trump side but not once you are on glacier ice.

Rockfall and icefall off the Wapowety Cleaver and the Kautz Icefall are the approach-zone hazards; move through the exposed ground early and efficiently.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-May to early Aug; the ice holds into summer but the approach and glacier conditions degrade quickly after the start of August
hazards: Two steep ice steps beneath serac and rockfall from the Wapowety Cleaver and the Kautz Icefall
Brittle or hard ice on the upper step, with screws the only protection
Genuinely complex crevassed glacier travel on the Kautz approach
A short rappel or fixed-line downclimb off the Camp Hazard bivy rock to reach the base
Descent rappels are on ice anchors you build yourself; old ascent-placed threads must not be reused
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The headwall and the standard Kautz Chute are two different lines off the same camp, and the test is how many steep steps you meet.

Count two. This route presents as two ice steps separated by a band of lower-angle snow: the lower step around 35-40 degrees, the upper around 45-50. Step, bench, step. If you climb one sustained runnel and the angle then eases the whole way to the summit plateau, you were in the standard Kautz ice chute, not on the headwall.

The upper step is the one that settles it — noticeably steeper and more sustained than the lower, needing two tools and screws in ice that is often harder or more brittle. The lower step is broad and stepped out and rarely steeper than about 35-40 degrees, and most parties get up it with a single tool and a couple of screws. If the harder ground came first, you are not on this.

Where you rope up is part of the finding: on the Turtle or Wilson Glacier below the headwall, often after a short rappel or a fixed-line downclimb off the bivy rock at Camp Hazard. Descending off camp before you climb is correct and is a good sign you are on the right line rather than walking out along the chute.

The approach has two starts and they land in the same place, so do not let the difference unsettle you: Paradise via Glacier Vista and the Nisqually Moraine, or the Comet Falls and Van Trump Park trail from a lower trailhead. Both cross the Nisqually onto the Wilson and climb the Turtle. If you find yourself on maintained trail beside a waterfall you are on the second of those, not lost.

What being too late looks like: seracs and rockfall off the Wapowety Cleaver and the Kautz Icefall hang over the steep ground. The upper step must be climbed efficiently and early. The honest reading of arriving at it warm and in the sun is to go down.

approach_variants.name: White Salmon Creek from the old lodge site, up the White Salmon Glacier to the dividing shoulder
approach_variants.notes: Get the backcountry permit at the Glacier Public Service Center on the way in — it is required, not advisory. Then continue up the Mount Baker Highway to the pull-off at the old White Salmon Lodge site, walk round the gate, and follow the old roadbed roughly a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. From the road-end, with adequate snow cover, drop northeast off-trail to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier. Roped travel usually begins at the toe, and the crevasse hazard grows through the season. Ascend glacier and moraine to a bivy below the first rock and ice barrier. Published bivy elevations for this route disagree by around a thousand feet — so the honest instruction is to camp at the rock outcrops on the eastern edge of the White Salmon, where the ridge meets the face, rather than at a number. The Hanging Glacier and North Face approach is in the White Salmon Creek drainage, one valley east of Price Lake — not on the Nooksack and Ruth Creek side of the mountain.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Aug. Earlier the valley is snow-covered and simpler but the true North Face above you sheds avalanches; later the crevasses on the White Salmon are open and the lower valley is alder
hazards: Frequent avalanches off the true North Face onto the traverse, worst in early season
Serac fall from the hanging glacier itself, which is described as very active
Open crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier that grow through the season
Brush and alder in the lower White Salmon valley once the snowline recedes
A traverse with no easy retreat once committed, and a bivy on the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Price Lake must stay below you and to your west, and that is the test. From the bivy the day is a traverse climber's left, above and across the hanging glacier that sits over Price Lake and beneath the upper hanging glacier tucked under the first rock barrier. In cloud you will not see the summit and you do not need to: the lake is the reference and it belongs on your left-hand side, downhill.

Arrival: you are at the base of the technical climbing when you reach the shoulder — the snow-and-ice rib that divides the White Salmon cirque from the Price Glacier cirque. It is the only place on this traverse where the ground stops being a sidehill and becomes a defined rib with a cirque falling away on each side. Stand on it and you should be able to look down into two separate basins.

The error that kills people here is drifting left, and it is worth stating as a hard rule: stay right during the traverse. Going further left puts you onto the true North Face, which sheds avalanches frequently, especially early season. Left feels like progress toward the mountain and is the wrong direction.

After 500 ft of traverse the line goes up, on a firn-and-ice finger west of the upper hanging glacier. If you are still traversing horizontally after a long way, you have gone past the finger and are running out under the face.

approach_variants.name: Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide, then down the White Salmon Glacier to the base
approach_variants.notes:
The alternative used by parties who would rather start from the standard trailhead than from the White Salmon roadbed: from the Lake Ann Trailhead on SR-542, climb the Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide to a bivy near the Upper Curtis Glacier, then descend about 1,000 ft down the White Salmon Glacier and traverse the northwest rib to reach the foot of the Hanging Glacier.

It is longer in vertical terms because it climbs to a camp and then gives back a thousand feet, and it commits you to regaining that thousand feet on the way out if you return the same way. Its advantage is a maintained trail to a known camp instead of a valley bushwhack, and it does not require the White Salmon roadbed to be walkable.

No trailhead-to-base time is given for this variant; published figures for it vary too much to quote one.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Aug, once the Lake Ann trail is out from under snow
hazards: A 1,000 ft descent that must be re-climbed on the return if you reverse this variant
Winnie's Slide, which is sometimes rappelled rather than downclimbed when icy
Crevasses on both the Lower Curtis and the White Salmon
Avalanche exposure from the true North Face during the traverse
Committing to a route whose descent normally exits a different valley from the one you started in
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You arrive from above, so the test is inverted — you are looking for the bottom of a descent, not the top of a climb. From the Upper Curtis bivy you drop roughly 1,000 ft down the White Salmon Glacier. Stop descending when the ground lets you traverse northeast onto the northwest rib; if you keep going down the White Salmon you end up in the valley the other variant walked up, and you will have thrown away the whole approach.

The rib is the marker. The northwest rib is a defined feature between the White Salmon and the Hanging Glacier, and once you are on it the foot of the Hanging Glacier is the next thing you meet.

Confirm with the same test the other variant uses: from the base of the climbing, Price Lake should be below you and to the west, and you should be standing on the shoulder that separates the White Salmon cirque from the Price cirque, with a basin on each side of you.

And the same hard rule applies: do not drift left onto the true North Face. It avalanches, and arriving from this side does not change that.

approach_logistics.trailhead: White Salmon Day-Lodge Area (FR-3075, Mt. Baker Ski Area)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the White Salmon day-lodge area on SR-542 (White Salmon Road, FR-3075), via the old roadbed into the White Salmon Creek drainage

approach_variants.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin camp
approach_variants.notes: Book a water taxi for the long run up Ross Lake and get dropped at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft; above that the route is cross-country with occasional blazes, across slide alder and forest slopes, to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft. This is the shorter side for this particular route and it keeps the whole trip inside the United States, at the cost of depending on a boat.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September
hazards: a booked boat on a lake with no road out
slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the old cabin
crevasses on the glacier above the col
a wide gully that collects anything falling from the slopes above it
a high camp with a long committing retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route starts at a col, not on a face, and the col is between two peaks. From the lake basin camp, gain the wide gully on the north side of the saddle and climb it to the col at about 7,380 ft between this peak and its neighbour to the north-west. The glacier route begins there.

Recognise the col by what is on both sides of it. You should be standing in a gap with a summit rising to either hand and ground falling away in front and behind. If the mountain is above you and there is nothing behind you but the slope you came up, you are on a shoulder rather than the col.

The gully is the positive marker on the way up - a wide one, on the north side of the saddle. A narrow gully, or one on the south side, is a different line.

And the negative marker that matters most: the south-west route on this peak starts at the toe of a different glacier on the other flank, reached by traversing round a rock buttress into heather and moraine basins rather than by gaining any col. If you are roping up at the foot of an icefall with no saddle in sight, you have started the other route.

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border, over the col between the two peaks
approach_variants.notes: The other way in starts on the Canadian side: a rough spur off the lake road to a washout at about 2,600 ft, an overgrown roadbed to the boundary obelisk and register, and then the climbers' path up the creek through old growth to the falls, whose wet slabs and old fixed hand-line are the crux of the walk-in. Above them the path leads to the lake camp at about 5,700 ft. From that camp the way to this route climbs toward and over the col between the two peaks rather than onto the south-west side.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, and only with passports
hazards: an international border crossing on foot
wet slabs and an old fixed hand-line at the falls
an overgrown approach road that washes out
crevasses on the ice above the col
two routes leaving one camp, with the wrong turn costing a day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the Depot Creek camp you are approaching the col from the opposite side, so descriptions written from the other camp will have the gully and the col in the wrong relative positions - read the ground rather than the page.

The fixed point is the same: the col at about 7,380 ft between this peak and its neighbour to the north-west. It is a gap with a summit on either hand and the glacier beyond. The wide gully on the col's north side is the connection to the basin on the far side.

The test that you are at the right gap is that both summits are identifiable from it, and that the ice you are about to climb runs away from the col rather than up to it. A notch with only one summit beside it, or with no glacier beyond, is a different gap on the same ridge.

Do not confuse this start with the south-west route, which leaves the same camp. That route turns right around the toe of a rock buttress well before any saddle and ropes up at the toe of a glacier on the other flank. If you have not gained a col, you are not on this route.

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
approach_variants.notes:
From the road washout at about 2,600 ft, reached by a rough spur off the lake road on the Canadian side, walk the old roadbed about nine minutes to an inconspicuous spur on the left, follow that spur four minutes to a T-junction, and bear right onto an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for about thirty-five minutes. That brings you to the boundary obelisk, where there is a register - carry a passport, because this approach crosses the international border on foot.

Above the boundary the way becomes a crude but discernible climbers' path along the creek through old growth, easy where deadfall has been cut and full of uncut logs where it has not. About three miles in it reaches the falls, which are the real crux of the approach: wet slick boulders and slabs at their base, with steep steps rigged with an old fixed hand-line. Treat the line as an aid rather than as protection, and back it up with a heavy pack on.

Above the falls the path continues through meadow and upper valley to the lake at roughly 5,700 ft - flat sandy mostly treeless benches at the toe of the talus, the standard base camp for this peak and its neighbour, with reliable water.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, for a crossable glacier and a passable creek
hazards: an international border crossing on foot, with a register at the obelisk
a road that washes out and lengthens the walk without warning
wet slick boulders and slabs at the base of the falls, with an old fixed hand-line of unknown condition
crevasses on the south-west glacier and one marginal snow bridge on the standard line
a short steep loose gully at the head of the glacier
thirty-five to forty degree snow near the summit ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The critical instruction is that you leave the drainage before the pass, not at it. From camp, ascend the broad talus couloir and stream drainage north to north-east toward the saddle at roughly 7,200 ft - but well before reaching that saddle, cut right around the toe of a steep rocky buttress into open heather and moraine basins.

The negative marker is exact and easy to use: if you have arrived at the saddle and are looking down into the cirque on the far side, you have gone too far. Go back down and find the buttress toe.

The buttress toe is the feature - a steep rock nose that the couloir runs past on its left. Turning its foot puts you into open heather and moraine, which is different ground from the couloir you have been climbing, and that change underfoot is the confirmation.

The base is the toe of the south-west glacier, reached by traversing those basins. Rope up and put crampons on there rather than part-way across.
