The line up the ice is its climber's-right margin, which holds hard snow and ice at thirty to forty degrees and relatively few crevasses; about half-way up, one poor-looking crevasse has to be crossed on a marginal bridge, so probe it and expect it to be worse late in the season.

Confirm at the top of the ice: a short steep loose rock gully at the glacier's head tops out on a low col on the south-west ridge, above the cirque. That col is where the summit scramble starts. If the ice runs you out onto a broad snow shoulder with no gully and no col, you have taken the glacier's centre or its left side instead of its right margin.

approach_variants.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin
approach_variants.notes:
The other side of the mountain is reached without leaving the United States. A booked water taxi runs a long way up Ross Lake to a drop at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek for roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft, above which the way is cross-country with occasional blazes across slide alder and forest slopes to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft.

This puts you on the opposite side of the peak from the Depot Creek camp, so it changes which col you reach and in what order - plan the climb from this camp rather than translating a description written from the other one.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the boat is running and the cross-country is clear of snow
hazards: a booked boat on a lake with no road out, fixing both ends of the trip
slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the cabin
a long carry to a high camp
crevasses on the glaciers either side of the divide
a camp position that makes descriptions written from the other approach misleading
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The old cabin at about 2,900 ft is the proof you are on the right side of the creek. The trail climbs the north side; if you have not passed a cabin by the time the trail gives out, you are on the wrong bank and should cross before the cross-country starts, not after.

Above the cabin the markers are occasional blazes on trees rather than tread. Blazes that stop appearing mean you have drifted; the slide alder will let you keep going anyway, which is why this is worth checking rather than assuming.

The camp is the lake basin at about 6,763 ft, and from it the route to this peak's south-west side goes up and over toward the col between it and its neighbour to the north-west.

Be clear which route you are on when you arrive. From this side the natural line gains the col at about 7,380 ft between the two peaks, which is where the glacier route on the north side starts. The south-west route instead wants the toe of the south-west glacier, which is reached by traversing into open heather and moraine basins round the toe of a rock buttress, not by gaining a col. If you find yourself standing in a saddle between two summits, you are on the other route's start.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Depot Creek Road trailhead (via Chilliwack, BC)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Chilliwack, BC via Chilliwack River Road ~31.7 miles, then the rough Depot Creek Road spur (high-clearance; passport required to cross the border on foot); unmaintained Depot Creek trail up-valley

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail from Hamma Hamma Road to Lake of the Angels
approach_variants.notes:
From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25) at about 1,565-1,600 ft — an unmarked roadside pullout, roughly 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake Trailhead — the Putvin Trail is an unmaintained, primitive user trail that climbs steeply and directly from the first steps. Expect root-staircase steps and boot-track tread through forest for the first mile. In recent years a slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles of road, adding a road-walk; check Forest Service status.

About halfway up the trail meets a rock headwall requiring hand-over-hand climbing, with a large tree root as the key handhold and, historically, a fixed handline on the steepest pitch. Above it the trail eases into subalpine forest and heather meadows, passing near Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet, and reaches Lake of the Angels at roughly 4,850-4,920 ft in a cirque below Mount Stone's south face — about 3 to 3.5 miles and 3,000 ft of gain. Little to no reliable water on the lower trail; carry enough to reach the lake.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow lingers in the basin above the lake well into summer
hazards: Trail-less, route-finding-dependent terrain above Lake of the Angels
Near-vertical root and rock steps on the lower Putvin Trail, genuinely exposed when wet, and worse descending on tired legs
Loose rock on the headwall and summit block with rockfall onto parties below
An ambiguous Class 3/4 crux near the summit
Fog is common here and multiple parties have lost the route on the upper mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the climb is a notch in Mount Stone's west ridge, and the test for it is a turn you make before a gate. From Lake of the Angels contour and climb toward St. Peter's Gate — the obvious notch above the basin. Just before the gate, turn sharply left (south) and traverse along the base of the cliffs to a notch in the west ridge. If you walk through St. Peter's Gate, you have gone too far; the Gate is the marker you turn short of, not the one you pass through. That works in cloud because the cliff base is a tactile handrail: once you have made the turn, you keep rock on one side of you the whole traverse. Lose contact with the cliff and you have drifted downhill. Second test, at the notch: turn right and climb toward a first sub-summit rock, then up a short low class 3 chimney to its top. A chimney is a shape you can feel with both hands. If the first difficulty above the notch is a face or a slab rather than a chimney you can bridge, you are not on the line. Third test, on the summit spire: from the sub-summit cross a brief, somewhat exposed ridge to the base of the true summit spire, then follow a groove on the left side that bends right, where a faint climbers' path leads the last steps to the top. Left then right — a groove that runs straight up is not it. What the route's own timing says: about 2.5 hours up from the Lake of the Angels camp and about 1.5 hours back down. If you have been on the ground above the lake far longer than that without finding the notch, you have most likely missed the turn short of the Gate. Fog warning specific to this mountain: Mount Stone has more than one summit, and parties have confused the true south summit with the Middle and North summits in cloud. Count your ridges.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and Upper Lena Lake, the St. Peter's traverse from the east
approach_variants.notes:
The other side of the same notch. From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FS 25 at roughly 600-750 ft, take the well-graded Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork Lena Creek drainage roughly 3.5 more miles to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft, some 6.5 miles and 4,000 ft from the trailhead. Upper Lena Lake is the last maintained-trail camp and the last reliable water before the traverse goes cross-country; wilderness permit and bear canister required.

From Upper Lena Lake, leave the trail and head west on the Scout Lake way-trail across meadows and heather past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down slightly to Upper Scout Lake, round it into Scout Basin, and up to Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above the tarns known as Ullin's Bathtubs. From there a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone that ends at a loose moraine, and then exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

This is a two- or three-day trip and it is chosen for the country it crosses, not because it is quicker.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the off-trail benches and passes are largely clear
hazards: Extensive off-trail way-trail route-finding over multiple passes and basins with faint tread
Loose glacial moraine of all sizes near St. Peter's Gate and exposed dirt-and-mud slopes on the final ramp
Fog on the upper mountain — multiple parties have lost the route here and ended up in harder terrain
No dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the tarns near Ullin's Pass
A very long approach with limited bail options partway through
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming from the east you arrive at St. Peter's Gate itself, which is the high point of the traverse at about 5,950 ft and an obvious rocky notch in Mount Stone's southeast ridge. That is the arrival test and it is unmistakable in any weather: the ground stops rising, the notch pinches, and the Lake of the Angels basin opens on the far side. From the gate there are two ways onto the peak and they are different climbs. The one this route describes is the west-ridge notch: go through the Gate and drop toward the Lake of the Angels basin, then work back up and turn the corner onto the cliff-base traverse to the notch in the west ridge — the same notch the Putvin parties reach by turning sharply left just short of the Gate. The other is the south-face gully, which starts by descending about 300 ft from the Gate to the base of a basalt cliff; that is the Lena Lake traverse route's line, not this one. So the fog test for this variant is which side of the gate you end up on: this route goes over to the Lake of the Angels side and approaches the west ridge from the south-west, keeping the cliff base at your shoulder. Above the notch the tests are identical to the Putvin variant: turn right, low Class 3 chimney to a sub-summit, a brief exposed ridge, then a groove on the left that bends right to the true south summit.

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail #813 to Lake of the Angels, then the traverse under the cliff band
approach_variants.notes: this route and the Lake of the Angels route appear to be the same climb entered twice. The variants here are written for the ground the route itself describes. Park at the Putvin Trailhead (FST 813) at about 1,565 ft on Hamma Hamma Road (FR 25). A slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles; check Forest Service status. The trail follows the west side of Boulder Creek a few hundred feet, then starts a long unrelenting climbing traverse west, gaining nearly 3,000 ft in under 4 miles without easing. Around 1.3 miles it crosses an old logging road, and the tread is easy to lose there — look for the continuation slightly downhill. Around 4,200 ft comes the short headwall with an old hand-line or a large exposed tree root as the handhold, the crux of the trail and a common turnaround point when wet. Maintained tread ends in a basin around 3.9 miles at about 4,500 ft, and a rougher way-trail continues up steep rocky ground to Lake of the Angels at about 4,900 ft near 4 miles.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Consolidated snow has been reported from about 4,500 ft up well into summer in the north-facing basin above the lake
hazards: Exposed scramble moves near the summit block and a 15-20 ft Class 4 crack step with no fixed anchor
Lingering steep snow in the north-facing basin above the lake into early-mid summer
Route-finding above Lake of the Angels is loose and nontrivial in cloud or fresh snow
The 4,200 ft headwall on the trail is greasy when wet and the hand-line is not maintained
The tread is easy to lose where it crosses the old logging road at about 1.3 miles
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climb starts where the trail ends, and the arrival test is a cliff band, not a summit view. From Lake of the Angels the route leaves any trail: a boot path climbs a couple of hundred feet toward St. Peter's Gate, and short of the gate you turn left along the base of the long cliff band. Rock wall at your shoulder on one side and scree dropping away on the other is a check you can make in cloud without seeing anything further. Second test: along the cliff base, Class 2-3 ground and a couple of narrow chutes lead up toward a notch on Mount Stone's west ridge, below the feature called St. Peter's Gate. Below, not through. St. Peter's Gate is the notch in the southeast ridge and it belongs to the traverse from Lena Lake; the notch you want is on the west ridge and sits lower and to the south of it. If you have walked up to a notch that opens onto an entirely different basin to the east, that is the Gate and you are past your turn. Third test, on the summit block: the final 150 to 200 ft is mostly Class 3 but contains one well-documented 15 to 20 ft class 4 step up a shallow crack, often marked by a cairn. A cairn is man-made and does not move. If you have reached the top without meeting a short crack step, you are on a sub-summit — this mountain has three, and parties confuse them in fog. What the route's own timing says: Mountaineers reports for this line log around 5.5 hours up and 4 hours down, roughly 10 hours car to car. Caution from a trip report, and it is route-finding advice rather than a hazard note: at least one party took a steep mossy waterfall gully as a descent shortcut and found it far worse than reversing the ascent. Reverse the cliff-base traverse; do not improvise a line down the south side.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and the St. Peter's traverse, arriving at the Gate from the east
approach_variants.notes:
The long way to the same mountain, kept here because it is a genuinely different approach rather than a variation of the Putvin walk. Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft and 6.5 miles. From there, off-trail west past Lena Tarn and Scout Lake to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down to Upper Scout Lake and round into Scout Basin, over Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above Ullin's Bathtubs, then a rising traverse to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone, ending on loose moraine, and finally exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

Most parties then continue southwest about half a mile into the Lake of the Angels basin, which is where this approach rejoins the Putvin ground, and exit down the Putvin Trail — a different trailhead about 4 road miles from Lena Lake, so plan a shuttle or a stashed bike.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Extensive off-trail route-finding across Scout Pass, Scout Basin and Ullin's Pass on faint tread
Loose glacial moraine and exposed dirt slopes below St. Peter's Gate
Requires a car shuttle or stashed bike between two trailheads about 4 road miles apart
Fog on the upper mountain, where parties have repeatedly lost the route
Unbridged stream crossings on the way-trail sections
approach_variants.baseFinding: The arrival test is St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft: the traverse's high point, an obvious rocky notch in Mount Stone's southeast ridge, reached up a steep snow-and-dirt ramp over loose moraine. Ground stops rising, notch pinches, and the Lake of the Angels basin opens beyond. The test that puts you on this route's line rather than the gully line: from the Gate, continue southwest into the Lake of the Angels basin and pick the route up from there — the traverse left along the base of the cliff band, and Class 2-3 ground to the notch on the west ridge below the Gate. The alternative from the Gate is to drop about 300 ft directly to the base of a basalt cliff and take the south-face gully; that is the Lena Lake traverse route, a Class 3-4 gully, and a different climb. Above the west-ridge notch the test is the same: a short Class 4 step up a shallow crack, often cairned, in the last 150 to 200 ft, on a mountain with three summits. Honest limit: coming from the east adds a day and several passes of unmarked way-trail. It is chosen for the country, not for the climb.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: Park at the Putvin Trailhead (FST 813, ~1,565 ft) on Hamma Hamma Road (FR 25)

approach_variants.name: North side — Stuart Lake TH via Mountaineer Creek
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR 7601 (Eightmile Road) out of Leavenworth and walk the Stuart Lake Trail up Mountaineer Creek. At the signed split roughly two miles along, ignore the Colchuck Lake branch on the right and carry straight on. A short distance further you leave maintained tread altogether, well before Stuart Lake, ford Mountaineer Creek and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. Late in the season there is a cairned climbers' path through much of this; early in the season there is not, and the creek runs hard.

Above the streamside travel a steep, unstable talus and boulder slope lifts you into the hanging basin under Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier. This basin holds the usual bivies. From it you angle up onto the glacier bench beneath the ridge.

This is the shorter, lower-gain way in and it puts you at the toe with the most in the tank, but it commits you to a car shuttle: the standard descent is the Cascadian Couloir, which spills out on the far side of the range at Ingalls Creek. Parties report the shuttle drive between the two trailheads costing several hours round trip. In June and early July the Sherpa Glacier is a reasonable way back down to this side and removes the shuttle problem — later in the summer it is not.

There is running snowmelt near the toe of the ridge (reported around 47.48095, -120.89454); above the 8,200 ft notch there is no reliable water once the last snow patch there melts out.
approach_variants.season: Jun to mid-Jul is the sweet spot; workable through Sep
hazards: Mountaineer Creek and its south fork run high and fast in early-season melt
Loose talus and boulder slope below the Sherpa Glacier basin — poor footing, rockfall onto parties below
Serac and icefall exposure if you drift east under the Ice Cliff Glacier
No reliable water above the 8,200 ft notch once its snow patch is gone
Committing: standard descent exits on the opposite side of the range, so a shuttle or a very long walk-around is required
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are climbing the complete North Ridge, which begins at about 6,600 ft — roughly 1,500 ft of roped ground below the point where most people who say 'North Ridge' actually start. The toe is the lowest rock of the rib that separates the two glaciers: Stuart Glacier on its west side, Ice Cliff Glacier on its east. Standing at the base with the Ice Cliff Glacier and its seracs on your left and the Stuart Glacier hidden around the corner to your right, you are in the right place. If you are underneath hanging ice you have drifted too far east onto the Ice Cliff side and need to come back west to the rib's lowest rock.

The feature to not mistake for the start is the notch at 8,200 ft. That notch is obvious — a saddle in the crest with a scatter of bivy platforms and, usually, a small lingering snowfield for water — and it is where the Upper (original) North Ridge begins. It is reached by a rock gully climbed from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at about 7,700 ft, on the ridge's west flank. If you find yourself scrambling a gully up from snow toward a bivy saddle, you have skipped the lower 1,500 ft and are on the Upper route, not the Complete.

In cloud, use the glaciers rather than the rock: the toe is where the moraine/snow of the basin runs out against the first continuous rock, and the ice above and left of you belongs to the Ice Cliff Glacier. The 8,200 ft notch is above and right of that, reached only after the ridge has already risen well above the ice.

approach_variants.name: South side — Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass and Goat Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), take the trail over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, then traverse east beneath the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe of the ridge.

About 2,000 ft of the day is descent, so the round trip is more work than the raw gain suggests, and parties consistently report it taking longer than planned — budget eight hours and expect route-finding on the traverse rather than tread.

The reason to accept the longer, higher approach is that it removes the shuttle entirely. The Cascadian Couloir descent drops to Ingalls Creek on this side, so a party that walked in from Esmeralda walks out to its own car. Parties who came in from the north do not.

How much snow remains on the Goat Pass traverse is the recurring gear question here: sections have been reported at around 40 degrees, and whether you need an axe and traction changes week to week through the summer. Recent photos and current reports are worth more than any fixed answer.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the traverse under the Stuart Glacier has melted or consolidated
hazards: Snow slopes on the Goat Pass traverse reported near 40 degrees; conditions change through the summer
~2,000 ft of descent on the way in, all of which must be regained on the way out
Long day with no bail-out once past Goat Pass
Approach consistently underestimated; parties arrive at the toe late and tired
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Coming from Goat Pass you arrive at the ridge from below and to the west, which is the opposite side from the northern approach — so the Ice Cliff Glacier is not your handrail here, the Stuart Glacier is. Keep the Stuart Glacier snow on your left as you traverse east and stay above the big moraine mound; the toe of the Complete ridge is the first continuous rock the traverse runs into, at about 6,600 ft.

The decision point is unmissable once you know to look for it: from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at roughly 7,700 ft a rock gully leads up the ridge's west side to the notch at 8,200 ft. Taking that gully puts you on the Upper North Ridge and skips the lower 1,500 ft. Continuing the traverse past and below it, down to the lowest rock, is what starts the Complete route. In poor visibility: if the snow you are standing on is still rising to your right toward a saddle, you are too high; the toe is below, where the snow ends.

approach_variants.name: Reached only by climbing the North Ridge — the base is a point on the route, not a place you walk to
approach_variants.notes:
There is no independent approach to this feature. The Great Gendarme is a tower high on Mount Stuart's North Ridge and you arrive at its base having already climbed either the complete ridge from the toe near 6,600 ft or the upper ridge from the notch above the Stuart Glacier. Reckon on roughly eight or nine pitches of ridge above the notch, and considerably more from the toe.

What matters at the Gendarme is the decision made at its base, because the Gendarme is the one place on the ridge where there is a real choice and where a party that has not decided in advance loses time at 9,000 ft.

Both options are established. The tower goes in two pitches — a lieback, then the offwidth — and it can also be turned on ledges to the west, which is what the original 1956 ascent did and what most parties still do. The bypass is not an escape hatch invented by tired climbers; it is the older line.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, as for whichever North Ridge line you are on
hazards: Arriving at the tower late in the day with the summit still above and no quick way off the ridge
1,000+ ft of exposure on both sides of the crest
Rockfall from parties above on a popular ridge
Cold wind, and an unplanned bivy if the choice at the base costs too long
Retreat from above the Gendarme is awkward in either direction
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are at the base when the ridge stops being scrambling and stands up in front of you. Everything below is fourth to mid-fifth class on excellent granite that you have been moving together on. The Gendarme is where that ends: a steep tower blocking the crest, roughly 500 ft below the summit, and there is nothing else on the ridge it can be confused with.

The discriminator is whether you can walk round it. If a line of ledges leads off left (west) and lets you keep moving without roping up properly, you are at the bypass — the same place, and the decision point. If you are looking straight up at a clean lieback flake with an offwidth above it, you are at the climb.

So the test in fog is a negative one, and it is worth stating because parties do get this wrong on the way to the summit: if you are still on the ridge and have not yet had to make that choice, the Gendarme is ahead of you and the summit is not. If you have made it and are back on blocky fourth and low-fifth ground, the Gendarme is behind you and the summit is close.

A useful sanity check on the two pitches themselves: the second one has a reputation far worse than the climbing, and parties consistently report it going on good holds and jams with fixed gear in it. If the offwidth you are in feels desperate and unprotectable, look again at where you are — you may have entered the wrong crack on the tower.

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek to the hanging valley, then straight to the toe of the ridge
approach_variants.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road (about 3,400 ft), follow the trail past the Colchuck Lake fork and keep going. Roughly a mile beyond that fork the maintained trail turns uphill and switchbacks away to the right for Stuart Lake. Leave it there and stay flat in the valley with Mountaineer Creek. Cross the creek on logs — there is no canonical log and the crossing moves with the snowpack — then follow the south fork upstream. After a couple of miles the valley steepens; turn up a steep talus and boulder slope into the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak, where the bivy sites are. That flat ground under the glaciers is the arrival cue for camp. From the hanging valley the last leg is a faint climbers' path through trees and talus to the moraine, then up the edge of the moraine to rock. The Direct start is the same climb as the Complete North Ridge with a lower-ridge variation on its first pitches; if you are looking at an entry on this app for 'North Ridge (Complete)' as well, treat the approach as identical.
approach_variants.season: Jun-mid Jul; best early, while the Sherpa Glacier still gives a straightforward descent back to this side
hazards: Log crossings of Mountaineer Creek that shift year to year and are worse under early-season snow
Rockfall and icefall off the Ice Cliff Glacier while traversing the moraine beneath it
An open moat between snow and rock at the toe late in the season
Loose rock and crumbly black lichen on the lower pitches
A committing 20-pitch route with the Great Gendarme high on it and no easy retreat once above the lower ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Keep the Ice Cliff Glacier on your left and walk until the rock stops you. That single sentence is the whole test, and it works in cloud because it is about which side the ice is on rather than about seeing the summit. Climbing out of the hanging valley towards the mountain, the Ice Cliff Glacier must stay on your left the whole way. If it swings round to your right you have walked past the toe and out onto the Stuart Glacier side.

The toe itself is the lowest rock of the ridge, at roughly 6,600 ft, where the moraine runs into the buttress. You are at the correct place when there is nothing lower to climb — the ridge above you rises unbroken and the ground on either side falls away into a glacier.

Second test, and it is what tells the Direct start from a wander onto the flank: the first belay is off a big ledge about 150 ft above the base of the toe, with a small tree on it. If you have not passed a big ledge with a tree inside the first rope length, you are not on the line. The three opening pitches are the hardest on the whole route — an awkward squeeze slot and then a long, sustained lieback crack on the left. If your first pitches feel easy, you have started too high and joined the ordinary ridge.

What going too far looks like: the ridge you are standing under gains a deep notch with flat bivy ground in it. That notch is where the Upper North Ridge starts, and reaching it on foot means you have skipped the 1,200 ft this route exists for.

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Lake and Goat Pass, traversing east below the Stuart Glacier to the toe
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, follow the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass and past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then pick up the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge and contour northwest to Goat Pass, about 7,600 ft — the col between Point 7893 and the West Ridge.

This is now the common way parties reach the ridge, and its advantage is that it puts you on the south side of the range where the descent also finishes, rather than committing you to a north-side camp you then have to walk back around to.

From Goat Pass, do not drop onto the glacier and go up. Traverse east below the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe.

Bivy sites exist at Goat Pass and at Stuart Pass. Published trailhead-to-base times for this variant vary widely enough that no figure is given here.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Ingalls Way trail is clear and the Stuart Glacier traverse is walkable
hazards: Crevasses and a soft afternoon snow surface on the Stuart Glacier traverse
Loose moraine and talus on the traverse below the glacier
Route-finding error at Goat Pass in cloud, where dropping onto the glacier feels natural and is wrong
A long committing route with the Great Gendarme high on it
No water between the last melt stream and the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Stay above the moraine mound and keep traversing. Coming from Goat Pass the mistake is vertical, not horizontal: the ground invites you to drop down onto the glacier or to climb up onto the ridge crest early, and both put you on the route above its start.

The line is a rising traverse east, above the large moraine mound below the Stuart Glacier, all the way to the toe. If you find yourself walking down onto flat glacier ice you have dropped too low. If you find yourself scrambling onto ridge crest before you have gone round the end of the rock, you are on the west flank and above the toe.

Arrival: the toe is the point where the buttress runs out into the moraine and there is nothing below it to climb, at roughly 6,600 ft. Confirm it the same way the north-side party does — from the toe, the Ice Cliff Glacier is on the far (east) side of the ridge and the Stuart Glacier is behind you to the west. If both glaciers are on the same side of you, you are not at the toe.

And the same first-pitch check applies: the opening belay is a big ledge with a small tree roughly 150 ft up, and the first three pitches are the hardest of the route. Easy first pitches mean you started too high.

approach_variants.name: Lyman Lakes basin to the south flank
approach_variants.notes: Access is the hard part and it has changed. The classic way in is by passenger ferry up Lake Chelan and a village shuttle to the Railroad Creek trail, then a long valley walk to the Lyman Lakes basin — but that corridor has been shut by flood and landslide damage with no near-term reopening, so plan instead on the longer route in from the Phelps Creek side over Spider Gap, which is eleven or twelve miles one way and involves glacier travel with an axe. Either way this is a camp-in-the-basin objective, not a day out. Maintained tread effectively ends at the lakes; everything above is picked by eye with no path and no cairns. It is commonly paired with the lower summit less than a mile to its south from the same camp.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September; axe early
hazards: Unconsolidated talus and scree with no path, releasing rock easily onto anyone below
A snowfield at the foot of the flank persists through late summer in most years
The lower southwest ridge is cliffed and drops off — it is not an ascent line from the basin
Extremely remote with access itself uncertain; confirm the corridor is open before committing
Glacier travel with moats and crevasses if you come over Spider Gap
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the Lyman Lakes basin the mountain shows as a broad talus flank above open meadow, and the base is a specific, findable thing rather than a general slope: a snowfield lying at roughly 7,000 ft at the foot of that flank, which survives into late summer most years and is visible as a white patch from the camps when you look up from the lake. Cross the meadow, round onto the south and southeast side, and climb to it. Above the snow a broad ledge leads rightward into the main gully, and the gully takes you to a notch on the crest from which the ridge runs to the top. Do not try to gain the crest lower down on the southwest side — that ridge is cliffed below the notch and the drop-offs are the reason parties are warned off it. The other thing to keep straight is which summit you are under: a lower, closer peak sits under a mile to the south, and if the ground ahead is easing toward a rounded top rather than steepening into a gully, you are on that one.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Whatcom Pass and Perfect Pass to a camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine
approach_variants.notes: The northern option, favoured by several recent parties. From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft, the Hannegan Pass Trail leads over the pass to the Chilliwack River Trail, which includes a cable-car crossing, then up the Brush Creek Trail to Whatcom Pass. From there the route leaves trail and goes off-trail via the Whatcom Glacier and Perfect Pass to a base camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. Expect 2-3 days of travel each way.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Aug
hazards: A bergschrund on the summit snow finger, crossed via a slabby rock step
Somewhat rotten rock on the summit tower and gully section, with natural anchors only
Rockfall off the buttress walls onto the snow finger
A 1,000 ft descending traverse that has to be regained on the return
The Chilliwack cable-car crossing and the Whatcom Glacier traverse on the way in
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start of the climbing is a saddle inside the buttress, at about 6,100 ft, and you get there by losing height first. From the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp, the way to Phantom is a roughly 1,000 ft descending traverse east across snow and talus to the base of Phantom's broad southwest buttress, then up a snowfield to a saddle around 6,100 ft within the buttress. That saddle is effectively the start of the technical climbing.

So the test in cloud is the shape of the ground, not the view: you go down and east for a thousand feet, then up a snowfield, and you stop when the snowfield delivers you into a gap in a rock rib rather than onto open mountainside. A saddle inside a buttress has rock rising on both sides of you; open snow does not.

What going too far looks like: continuing the descending traverse east past the buttress toe drops you toward Luna Cirque and the ground the peak's other route uses, which is a different climb from a different camp.

Confirm on the climb: above the saddle the route takes a pocket glacier and snowfield to a bergschrund crossed by a slabby rock step, then a snow finger, then broken class 2-3 rock to a false summit and a short exposed step to the true summit. One bergschrund, one snow finger, one false summit. If you have crossed two schrunds you are not on this line.

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver Trail to Luna Camp, then the Luna Creek bushwhack up Phantom's south side
approach_variants.notes: The line the recorded distance reflects. From Ross Lake Resort, take the water taxi across Ross Lake, roughly $35 and saving about 6 miles, to the Big Beaver trailhead. From there it is about 9 to 10 miles of maintained, mostly flat, forested trail up the Big Beaver Creek drainage through old-growth cedar and past beaver ponds to Luna Camp, an established backcountry site where a wilderness permit is required. From Luna Camp the trail effectively ends. Climbers leave the tread and push cross-country up the Luna Creek drainage toward Phantom's south side, gaining roughly 4,000 ft over a few miles through some of the worst brush in the Cascades. Modern parties report huckleberry, devil's club, vine maple and slide alder dense enough that half a mile an hour is a good pace, with heavy insect pressure.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Aug
hazards: Some of the worst brush in the Cascades, at roughly half a mile an hour, with devil's club and slide alder
Fords of Luna Creek that get harder the lower you are
High risk of falling into a hole hidden by brush, and of separating from a partner
Heavy mosquito and fly pressure in summer
No trail, no cairns and real disorientation on the way back down
approach_variants.baseFinding:
In this drainage the navigation rule is about height, not direction, and it is the one thing that makes the day work. The creek must be forded in places, and fords get harder the lower and farther downstream you are. Gain elevation out of the valley bottom as early as you can rather than fighting the brush along the creek. If you are still beside running water after a couple of hours, you are on the losing line.

Arrival, which is unambiguous even with no visibility: above the brush line the drainage opens into subalpine meadow and talus below Phantom's south aspect. The brush stopping is the signal. Nothing else in this valley changes character that completely.

From there the base test is the same one the northern approach uses: find the snowfield that leads up into a saddle at about 6,100 ft within the southwest buttress. That gap is where the technical climbing starts.

A real risk peculiar to this approach, recorded because it has happened: in brush this thick, parties have become separated from each other. Agree a regrouping rule before entering it, not during.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to the Core, dry conditions
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the signed junction, and about four miles and 2,200 ft to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Filter here; there is nothing simple above until the Core.

Skirt the east and south shore to the boulder field at the lake's south end and start up Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000-2,200 ft in under a mile, on what regulars fairly describe as a jenga pile. Follow the outlet drainage and stay climber's left (east) of the first band of cliffs. Veering climber's right toward the waterfall complex on Colchuck Peak's flank is the classic and repeatedly fatal error here — people have died on that side and it cliffs out easily. Near the top the path passes in front of a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much larger one; missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Cairns are everywhere on Aasgard and they mark more than one line. Trust the worn tread over the cairn.

Top out around 7,800-7,841 ft, then lose 600-700 ft east and south through the Core's tarns and slabs to Prusik Pass. In the Core there are a couple of places where it is easy to add distance without adding progress, but the navigation is not hard in clear weather.

Most parties do this car-to-car, and a fit team should expect a 20-21 hour day; the Enchantments overnight permit lottery is competitive enough that camping is not a plan you can rely on.
approach_variants.season: late Jul-Sep, once Aasgard Pass is bare talus
hazards: Aasgard Pass: veering climber's right into the cliffed waterfall terrain has killed people
Loose talus and rockfall the full length of Aasgard, worse in the afternoon heat
Misleading and multiplying cairns on the pass and in the Core
No water between Colchuck Lake and the Core tarns
Very long day; parties routinely finish the descent of Aasgard in the dark
Descent from Prusik is rappels, not a walk-off — do not arrive without the gear
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the highest point of Prusik Pass, do not go over the first bump in front of you — go around it. Parties who climb straight over it lose time and, more importantly, lose the path.

Past the bump the climbing line drops out of sight. Keep scrambling easy blocky class 2 ground and it reappears. The landmark you are heading for first is a huge balanced, dish-shaped rock — that is the right place to stash packs and put on shoes, and it is not yet the start of the climbing.

One more knob of scrambling past that brings you to the actual base: an overhanging rock at the foot of the route, which is the natural sheltered spot to leave big bags.

The first pitch is the final confirmation and it is unmistakable even in cloud: a long pitch up a wide crack, about 5.6, in a conspicuously white section of rock. The white band is the marker — the surrounding stone is not that colour. A distinct crack of roughly 5.6 leading up through blocky ground to the ridge is what you want; if you are staring at clean, hard, featureless granite you are on one of the south-face routes instead.

Belay at a slingable block; the 5.7 slab crux with an old piton comes above that.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass with snow, early season
approach_variants.notes:
Same line, different problem. With snow on it, Aasgard is an axe-and-sometimes-crampons proposition rather than a talus grind, and it is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Early-season snow softens through the day into deep, punchy stuff that hides ice underneath, and the hidden creek running beneath the talus is a real hazard where snow bridges it. The consolidated dawn snow that makes the ascent quick is also the surface that makes an uncontrolled slide easy.

On the plus side the route-finding is simpler with the talus buried, and the Core beyond the pass travels fast on snow.

On the north side of Prusik itself, snow adds both hazard and time to the rappel descent — budget for it.
approach_variants.season: May-early Jul, while the pass holds continuous snow
hazards: Avalanche terrain on Aasgard Pass in shoulder season
Hidden creek running beneath the talus under snow bridges
Punchy afternoon snow concealing ice
Uncontrolled slide on the pass, ascending or descending
Snow on Prusik's north side lengthens and complicates the rappel descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Prusik Pass landmarks survive the snow, because they are large rock features: go around the first bump rather than over it, find the huge balanced dish-shaped rock to gear up at, then one more knob to the overhanging rock at the base.

The first pitch's white rock band and wide 5.6 crack still identify the start. What changes early season is the ground below the base — snow can cover the scrambling approach entirely, so the sequence of bump, dish rock, knob, overhang is what you navigate by rather than any boot path.

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek Trail #705 (FR 4096)
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mountain Loop Highway take FR 4096, a rough narrow spur where high clearance genuinely helps, to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft. Distance and gain above are the full round trip by this line.

Walk the old Bedal Creek trail roughly 1.5 miles and 700 ft. It is overgrown in stretches but stays followable. The critical junction is around 3,500 ft, where a climbers' path turns off to the left near 48.0560, -121.3631; it has carried pink flagging tape in recent years. Missing that turn is the standard error here — the old tread continues and dies in a brushy washout below the basin.

The climbers' path gains about 1,400 ft steeply through forest. At roughly 4,900 ft it breaks out into talus, then bends southeast through meadow and scattered timber to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft, where a shallow, somewhat stagnant pond marks the usual camp. This is the last easy water; cascading streams just below the saddle are the alternative.

Southeast from the saddle the ground opens into scramble terrain. At about 5,800 ft you cross a minor rock ridge and get your first view of the glacier. Snow from here is often firm in the morning and may want axe and crampons.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the forest band below 4,900 ft is clear of snow
hazards: Losing the 3,500 ft climbers'-path junction and ending in the brushy washout
Firm early-morning snow on the open slopes above 5,800 ft
Crevasses on the Sloan Glacier, normally bridged but open in lean years
Rough, narrow FR 4096 access spur
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Corkscrew does not begin at the glacier — it begins after you are off it. Cross the Sloan Glacier and keep going until you are standing on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block, around 7,300 ft; that bare-rock arrival is where parties cache rope, axe and crampons, and it is the single most reliable confirmation on the route. From there a boot track runs along heather ledges for ten to fifteen minutes. Watch to your right for a gully of pale, near-white rock and take that. Two negatives to check yourself against: if you are still on snow or ice you have not reached the start, and if you have walked the heather for much more than a quarter hour with no white-rock gully on the right, you are contouring too low — climb.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk / Cougar Creek (FR 49)
approach_variants.notes:
The start is an unsigned climbers' pullout on FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road) at roughly 1,900 ft, on the north side of the North Fork Sauk. It is not the maintained North Fork Sauk River Trail #649 — that is a different trailhead a short distance back along the road, and taking it is the common mistake.

The path runs flat and brushy through stinging nettle and then devil's club for a few tenths of a mile before dropping to the river. The river must be forded or crossed on a log jam; jams are usually adequate around half a mile in but shift from year to year and are a poor bet in high water. The path then crosses river braids two or three times over the next mile before turning up Cougar Creek on a faint, intermittently cairned and flagged track through sandy streambed and forest.

Around 3,000-3,200 ft the path crosses Cougar Creek itself; lower crossings can be impassable, so hold out for the 3.2K-ish one. Steep forest switchbacks follow, passing a waterfall on Cougar Creek near 5,000 ft — roughly two to two and a half hours from the car and the last reliable water before the basin. Above the falls the track leaves the trees onto scree and slabs and angles up to the 5,800 ft basin on Sloan's northeast side, where there is a small stream and the standard bivy. This line converges with the Bedal Creek approach around 5,000-5,500 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Aug, after the North Fork Sauk drops from snowmelt flow
hazards: Fording or log-crossing the North Fork Sauk — deep, cold and fast in early season
Log jams that move year to year and cannot be relied on
Devil's club and nettle on the lower path
Faint, easily lost tread up the Cougar Creek streambed
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same as the Bedal line: from the basin, ledges and slabs lead to the toe of the Sloan Glacier — rope and gear up there, not earlier. The climbing begins only once you are back on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block near 7,300 ft, and the entry is the gully of pale rock on your right, ten to fifteen minutes along the heather ledges from where you leave the ice.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Sloan Peak climbers' pullout (FR-49, Sloan Creek Road)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the unsigned Sloan Peak climbers' pullout on FR-49 (Sloan Creek Road, ~1,900 ft), crossing the North Fork Sauk River

approach_variants.name: Tunnel Creek trail to the crest trail at the lake, then south to the pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the forest road east of Skykomish, the Tunnel Creek trail climbs about eleven hundred and seventy feet in under a mile and a half from roughly 3,100 ft to a small lake on the crest, where it meets the long-distance crest trail. Turn south and follow that trail several miles to the pass at roughly 5,800 ft.

This is the option with the least climbing and the easiest tread. It is a little longer along the crest than the other trailhead, and the walking is straightforward the whole way, which makes it the better choice with heavy loads or a late start.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the crest trail is clear
hazards: an unmaintained ridge path beyond the pass with no signage
a long enough round trip that many parties camp, so a day attempt commits to a late finish
loose rock on the tower and on the ridge approach to it
a two-pitch face that still needs a rope, a rack and a plan to get back down
no water on the ridge between the pass and the tower
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The pass is the gate and the climbers' path leaves directly from the top of it. Do not look for it below the pass or beyond it: an unmaintained path runs south along the ridge from the pass itself. If you are casting about on the trail below the pass for a junction, you have not got high enough.

The tower is a distinct rock tower on that crest and it is the first one. The face you want looks back toward the pass on the north-east side, so from the path it presents itself as you approach rather than after you have passed it.

The critical negative marker is the mountain further along the same ridge. If you have walked past the tower and are looking at a broad peak with a lake basin below it, you have continued to the mountain and gone past the tower. Turn round; the tower is a slender formation and the mountain is not.

The route confirms itself on the second pitch: two pitches of easy fifth class, with the upper one diagonalling left into a gully and finishing at a large boulder near the top. A line that runs straight up with no leftward gully, or that takes more than a couple of pitches, is not this face.

One more caution about names: there are several mountains called Thunder in this state and more than one formation of this sort on crest trails. The identifying combination here is a pass on the long-distance crest trail with an unmaintained path leaving its top southward, and a tower standing before the mountain on the same ridge.

approach_variants.name: Surprise Creek trail past the two lakes, then the switchbacks to the pass
approach_variants.notes:
The other trailhead climbs the Surprise Creek trail past the first lake at about 4,500 ft and its neighbour, then switchbacks up to the same pass. It is roughly a mile shorter to the pass than the crest-trail option and costs several hundred feet more climbing, and it is in the trees for essentially the whole way, so it gives less to look at and less warning of the weather ahead.

Both trailheads meet at the pass and nothing above it differs.
approach_variants.season: July through September
hazards: more climbing than the other trailhead for a slightly shorter distance
forested trail the whole way, with little view of conditions ahead
an unmaintained ridge path beyond the pass
loose rock on the tower
no water on the ridge beyond the pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the pass the approach is identical to the other trailhead's: an unmaintained climbers' path leaves the top of the pass and runs south along the ridge.

The tower is the first distinct rock formation on that crest, and its north-east face looks back toward the pass. Because this approach arrives at the pass from below and in trees, take a moment on the pass itself to pick the tower out along the crest before starting the path - it is much harder to identify from underneath.

The negative marker is the same and it is the one that matters: the mountain lies further along the same ridge, above a lake basin. A broad peak with lakes below it is not the tower. If you are walking under a mountainside rather than under a slender formation, you have gone too far.

Confirm on the climb itself: two pitches of easy fifth class with the second diagonalling left into a gully to a large boulder near the top. If your first pitch is hard or your route runs straight up a face for several rope lengths, you are not on it.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Tunnel Creek or Surprise Creek Trailheads (US-2)

approach_variants.name: From the west: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack River Trail and Brush Creek to Whatcom Pass
approach_variants.notes:
About 16-17 miles one-way. Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, at about 3,100 ft, and follow Trail #674 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass, then descend the far side to Boundary Camp in the Chilliwack River valley.

Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail, unmaintained and rough in sections with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris, past Copper Creek Camp, then turn up at the Brush Creek Trail junction and climb through US Cabin Camp, Graybeal Camp and Whatcom Camp to Whatcom Pass. A cable-car crossing of the Chilliwack exists near U.S. Cabin Camp as an alternative to fording. Typically split over two days with a valley-bottom camp.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class choss in the final several hundred feet below the summit
Downclimbing that ground with an overnight pack, which reports rate as the riskier option
An unmaintained Chilliwack River Trail with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris
No fixed anchors anywhere on the ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the broad toe of the ridge, and you find it by walking south off the pass until the path dies. From Whatcom Pass a faint, informal climbers' trail leaves the maintained trail and heads directly south, gaining the broad toe of Whatcom Peak's north ridge. The path quickly gives way to snow patches and broken rock, and from there the route-finding rule is stay on the crest rather than follow any marked line.

So the fog test is a handrail test, and it is the best kind: once you are on the crest, keep it under your feet. Any time you find yourself sidehilling with the crest above you, you have come off it. There is nothing to identify on this ridge except the ridge.

Arrival at the start: you are on the route as soon as the informal path stops being a path and the ground becomes broken rock rising to a crest. That transition happens within a few hundred feet of the pass; this is not a route with a long walk to its base.

What the upper ridge is like, because it decides whether you come back this way: the final several hundred feet below the summit are described bluntly by climber reports as a chossy nightmare of loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class terrain, and downclimbing it with a heavy overnight pack is considered the harder, riskier option even though it is shorter. Many parties instead go over the summit and down the South Spur side.

And the other thing this ridge is: it is the direct line from Whatcom Pass to Perfect Pass that Challenger parties are told not to take. It is loose, extremely exposed and called a formidable obstacle. If you are on it as a shortcut rather than as your objective, you have chosen the wrong tool.

approach_variants.name: From the east: Ross Lake water taxi to Little Beaver, then 16 miles up-valley to Whatcom Pass
approach_variants.notes: Comparable in mileage to the western line. Hire a water taxi from Ross Lake Resort, near Diablo off SR-20, to the Little Beaver Creek trailhead at about 1,600 ft on Ross Lake, then follow the Little Beaver Trail roughly 16 miles up-valley, passing Perry Creek Camp at 4.6 miles and Twin Rocks Camp around mile 8, then the Big Beaver Trail junction at 10.5 miles, before the final steep switchback climb through big-fir forest up to Whatcom Pass.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A 16-mile valley walk that depends on a water-taxi booking at both ends
The same loose upper ridge as the western approach
Returning over the summit strands you on the wrong side of the peak from this trailhead
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Whichever way you arrive at Whatcom Pass, the base test is identical: leave the maintained trail, head directly south on the faint climbers' path, and stay on the crest once the path dies. The two approaches differ only in how you get to the pass.

The one thing this side changes, and it is a logistics fact rather than a navigation one: your car is at Ross Lake, not at Hannegan. That rules out the common descent option of crossing the summit and coming down the South Spur side to Perfect Pass, unless you are prepared to loop back around the peak's east side or across the Whatcom Glacier to regain Whatcom Pass.

How you know you are at the pass and not at a camp below it: the last stretch from the Big Beaver junction is a steep switchbacking climb through big fir. The pass is where that climb stops.
